4wd-light.look: An amber box with '4WD' or '4x4' inside it, or the letters 'AWD', usually low in the gauge cluster. Many trucks print words in the message area instead: 'Service 4WD', 'Service Four Wheel Drive', or '4WD system fault'. Subaru shows an AWD warning, and some SUVs use an outline of a car with the wheels and both axles picked out.
4wd-light.flash: A blinking 4WD symbol usually means the system is trying to shift and has not made it, so it is stuck part way between two-wheel and four-wheel drive. On some trucks it also blinks when the transfer case has got hot from spinning the wheels and the system has shut itself down to cool off.

diy.t: Check all four tires match and are properly inflated
diy.how: Read the size off the sidewall of each tire. The numbers must be the same on all four, and on a four-wheel drive they should be worn down about the same too. Then set every tire to the pressure listed on the sticker in the driver's door opening, using a gauge at a gas station. One odd-sized or badly worn tire makes the wheels turn at different speeds, and the 4WD computer reads that as a fault.

diy.t: Shift through the ranges, then restart
diy.how: Stopped on level ground with the transmission in park, move the 4WD switch or lever through each position, pausing a few seconds at each, then put it back to normal two-wheel drive. Shut the engine off, wait a minute, and start it again. If the light came on because a shift did not finish, or because the fluid had not circulated in a system that is rarely used, this sometimes clears it. The owner's manual gives the exact procedure for your car.

diy.t: Look for fluid drips beneath the middle of the truck
diy.how: Park on clean dry pavement for an hour, then stand beside the truck and look at the ground below its middle and rear. Do not crawl anywhere. Thick dark oil with a sharp smell points to a leaking transfer case or differential, and low fluid on its own is enough to set this light.

diy.t: Check the fuse for the 4WD system
diy.how: The owner's manual lists which fuse box holds it, usually the one inside the cabin by the driver's footwell or at the end of the dash. The lid has a map naming the 4WD or transfer case fuse. Pull that one with the plastic puller clipped inside the box and hold it up to the light: a broken metal strip inside means it has blown. Only ever fit the same amp rating.
diy.tools: Fuse puller from the fuse box

dont: Don't use 4WD or tow with this light on. The system can grab or let go without warning.
Don't keep driving on dry pavement if the truck feels stuck in four-wheel drive; it binds the driveline and breaks parts.
A mismatched rolling size sets this light again.
Don't rely on 4WD in snow until it has been checked, even if the light is the only sign of trouble.

causes2.name: Transfer case shift motor or actuator failed
causes2.tell: Four-wheel drive will not engage at all, or the indicator just blinks while the truck stays in two-wheel drive. You may hear a whirring or a clunk from the middle of the vehicle when you select it. Codes in the C0327 or P0833 range are common.
causes2.fix: Replace the shift motor or actuator on the transfer case, then relearn its position with a scan tool.

causes2.name: Front axle or hub engagement actuator
causes2.tell: A grinding or ratcheting noise from the front wheels when 4WD is selected, and the front wheels never pull. On many Fords these are small vacuum-operated units at the hubs; on GM and Toyota it is an electric actuator on the front axle.
causes2.fix: Replace the hub units or the axle actuator, and on vacuum systems the cracked hoses and the solenoid that feed them.

causes2.name: Mismatched or badly worn tires
causes2.tell: The light showed up within days of a new tire, a different size, or the spare being fitted. Nothing else is wrong and four-wheel drive still works. A shop can measure the rolling size of all four tires in minutes.
causes2.fix: Match all four tires for size and tread depth, often a pair or a full set, then have the code cleared.

causes2.name: Wheel speed sensor failed
causes2.tell: The ABS and traction control lights are nearly always on with it, and the speedometer may flicker or drop to zero. A scan tool names which wheel is not reporting.
causes2.fix: Replace the sensor at that wheel, or repair its wiring where it flexes near the suspension.

causes2.name: Low or old transfer case or differential fluid
causes2.tell: A whine, or a shudder in tight turns, with 4WD slow to engage. There is often a damp oily film around the case or a seal. Common on vehicles where four-wheel drive is almost never used.
causes2.fix: Drain and refill with the exact fluid the maker specifies, and replace the leaking seal if there is one.

causes2.name: 4WD selector switch or control module
causes2.tell: Turning the dial or pressing the button does nothing at all: no indicator, no noise from underneath. A shop separates the two by testing whether the switch signal reaches the module.
causes2.fix: Replace the selector switch, or the transfer case control module, which usually has to be programmed to the vehicle.

4wd-light.shop: A shop plugs in a scan tool first and reads the transfer case or 4WD module for stored codes, then measures tire sizes and tread, because a mismatch on its own sets this light. From there it commands the transfer case to shift while watching whether the motor actually moves and the position switches report back, and checks the power, ground and wiring to the actuator and the selector switch. Half an hour to an hour and a half is typical, longer if the fault comes and goes.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a service reminder. A scan tool will switch it off and the dash will look normal for a few minutes, but as soon as the system tests itself or you select four-wheel drive it comes straight back, because nothing has been repaired. Clearing it only belongs at the end of the job, once the real cause is fixed, and on most vehicles the light then goes out by itself after a few drives.
reset.note: A new shift motor or control module usually also needs a position relearn with a scan tool, and the procedure differs by make and model.

faqs.q: Can I keep driving with the 4WD light on?
faqs.a: On dry paved roads, yes. The vehicle normally falls back to two-wheel drive and drives as usual. What you have lost is four-wheel drive for the moment you need it, so get it looked at before the weather turns or before you tow anything.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive in snow with this light on?
faqs.a: Treat the vehicle as two-wheel drive and plan for that: more following distance, gentle throttle, winter tires if you have them. The bigger worry is the system engaging or dropping out on its own in a corner, which is unsettling on a slick road.

faqs.q: Will the 4WD light fail an inspection?
faqs.a: In most US states no, because it is not an emissions light and is not on the safety list. A few states note it on a safety inspection, and it will always show up on a pre-purchase or fleet inspection.

faqs.q: Will it go off by itself?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the cause was a shift that did not finish, or fluid that had not circulated in a system left unused for months, the light can clear after a stop and a restart. If it keeps coming back something is genuinely failing, and the codes stored in the module will say what.

faqs.q: Can one new tire really cause this?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is a common cause on four-wheel drive vehicles. A tire with more tread turns at a slightly different rate than the other three, so the computer sees front and rear speeds that do not agree and flags a fault even though every part is fine.

abs-light.look: An amber or yellow light in the instrument cluster, usually a circle with the letters ABS inside it and a curved bracket on each side. Some makes drop the circle and just show ABS in plain amber letters, and some trucks and European cars print a message such as ABS fault or Anti-lock brakes instead. It is normal for it to glow for a second or two when you first start the car and then go out.

diy.t: Switch the car off and start it again
diy.how: Turn the engine off, open and close the driver's door, wait about half a minute, then start it again and watch the light. Every car runs a quick self-test of the anti-lock brakes at start-up, and a one-off glitch, often from a weak battery or a brief wet connector, will not come back. If the light returns straight away, the car is finding a real fault.

diy.t: Look at the brake fluid level
diy.how: With the engine off and cool, open the hood and find the small see-through tank against the firewall on the driver's side. Read the level through the side of it without opening the cap; it belongs between the MIN and MAX marks. Low fluid can switch the anti-lock system off on its own, and it matters far more than the amber light does.

diy.t: Check your tires are the right size and properly inflated
diy.how: Read the size printed on the side of each tire and make sure all four match what the sticker in the driver's door frame calls for, with the front pair the same as each other and the rear pair the same as each other. Then set the pressures to that sticker with a gauge. The system works by comparing how fast each wheel turns, so one odd-sized or very soft tire can upset it.

diy.t: Look at the sensor wire behind each front wheel
diy.how: With the car parked and off, turn the steering fully to one side and look into the wheel well at the back of the brake disc. You should see a thin wire clipped along the suspension to a small sensor. Look only, and do not pull on it. A wire hanging loose, rubbed bare or chewed by an animal is the kind of thing that sets this light off, and it is worth pointing out to the shop.

diy.t: Note what else lights up and when
diy.how: Write down whether the traction control or stability light came on at the same time, whether the red brake light is on too, and whether the amber light appears the moment you start the car or only after a few minutes of driving.

dont: Don't assume the car stops as well as it used to on wet or icy roads. Without anti-lock brakes a hard stop can lock the wheels and you lose steering while they are locked.
Don't ignore it if the red brake light comes on as well. That combination is a brake problem, not just a switched-off safety feature, and the car should not be driven.
Don't pull the ABS fuse or cover the light to make it go away. You still have the fault, and now you have no warning of the next one.
Don't test it by slamming the brakes on a public road. Leave extra following distance instead and get the codes read.

causes2.name: A failed wheel speed sensor
causes2.tell: This is the common one. The stored code names a single wheel, such as left front or right rear. Alongside the amber light, the speedometer may jump about, the anti-lock brakes may buzz and pulse at walking pace when you are only parking, and the traction control light often comes on too.
causes2.fix: The one sensor at that wheel is unbolted and replaced. On most cars it is a bolt-in part and a short job, though a few makes build it into the wheel bearing.

causes2.name: Damaged sensor wiring or a corroded connector
causes2.tell: The light comes and goes rather than staying on, often appearing over bumps, in heavy rain, or only once the steering is turned. The code reads as an open or shorted circuit at one wheel. Looking in the wheel well you may see a chafed wire or a connector green with corrosion.
causes2.fix: The damaged length of wire or the connector plug is repaired or a new pigtail is spliced in, then the harness is clipped back where it cannot rub.

causes2.name: A damaged tone ring or a worn wheel bearing
causes2.tell: The tone ring is the toothed ring the sensor counts as the wheel spins. When its teeth rust away or get knocked about, the signal goes erratic rather than disappearing, so the light tends to come on above a certain speed. A humming or growling that changes as you steer left and right points at the bearing it sits in.
causes2.fix: The hub and bearing assembly, which usually carries both the ring and sometimes the sensor, is replaced as one unit.

causes2.name: Low brake fluid or another brake system fault
causes2.tell: The red brake warning light is on at the same time as the amber ABS light, and the fluid in the tank under the hood is at or below the MIN mark. The anti-lock system switches itself off when it cannot trust the brake pressure it has to work with, so the amber light here is a side effect.
causes2.fix: The real brake problem is fixed first, whether that is worn pads, a leaking line or a failing master cylinder, and then the fluid is topped and the system bled.

causes2.name: A failing ABS control module or pump
causes2.tell: The codes point at the unit itself rather than at any one wheel, the light is on from the moment the car starts and never varies, and the traction and stability lights usually come on with it. Sometimes there is a buzz or clunk from the unit under the hood when you first drive off.
causes2.fix: The module, the computer and pump that work the anti-lock brakes, is rebuilt or replaced, and the new one has to be coded to the car.

causes2.name: A weak battery or poor charging
causes2.tell: The ABS and traction lights flash up while the engine is cranking slowly, or after the car has sat for a few days, and clear once it has run for a while. Headlights may dim at idle. The anti-lock computer drops out when the voltage sags and reports a fault for it.
causes2.fix: The battery is tested and replaced if it is weak, or a charging fault at the alternator is sorted out, and the stored code is cleared.

abs-light.shop: A shop plugs a scan tool into the anti-lock brake computer and reads the stored code, which usually names the wheel that went quiet. Then they watch all four wheel speeds live on a short drive and see which one drops to zero or jumps around while the car is clearly moving. From there they go to that wheel and check the sensor, its toothed ring and the wire running to it. They also check the fluid level and battery voltage first, since both can switch the system off on their own. That is normally half an hour to an hour.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a reminder, so there is nothing you are meant to reset. A scan tool can clear the code and the light will go out, but the car tests the anti-lock system every single time you start it, and the light comes back on the next drive while the fault is still there. Once the sensor, the wire or the fluid is put right, most cars turn the light off by themselves after a short drive at normal road speed.
reset.note: Some makes hold the light on after the repair until a scan tool clears the old code, so a shop visit may be needed even when the part has been fixed.

faqs.q: Do my brakes still work with the ABS light on?
faqs.a: Usually, as long as the red BRAKE light is off and the pedal feels normal. The ordinary brakes are separate from the anti-lock system, which is why this light is amber, not red. What you have lost is the anti-lock part, the bit that stops the wheels locking up in a panic stop. Leave more room, brake earlier and more gently, and get it looked at soon. If the red BRAKE light comes on too, or the pedal feels soft, stop and have it towed.

faqs.q: Will I fail inspection with the ABS light on?
faqs.a: In many states that run a safety or emissions inspection, an illuminated ABS light is a fail, and in states with an OBD scan the stored brake code can fail it too. Rules vary by state and some older vehicles are exempt, so check your own state's list, but expect to fix it first.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive with the ABS light on in rain or snow?
faqs.a: It is riskier than usual, and that is the part people underestimate. With the anti-lock system off, a hard stop on a wet or icy road can lock the wheels, and locked wheels will not steer. Slow down, double your following distance, and brake in steady light pressure rather than one hard push.

faqs.q: The ABS light came on right after I had tires or wheels done. Why?
faqs.a: Wheel work is a very common trigger. A sensor wire can be knocked loose or pinched, a sensor can be left unplugged, or a mismatched or wrong-size tire can upset the wheel speed comparison. Go back to whoever did the work first and ask them to check their own job before paying for diagnosis.

faqs.q: Will the ABS light go off by itself?
faqs.a: Sometimes, if the cause was temporary, such as a weak battery or a wet connector that has dried out. If the fault is still there, it will not clear, and clearing the code without repairing anything just buys you one quiet drive. A light that goes off and comes back is still telling you something is wrong.

battery-light.look: A small red box in the instrument cluster shaped like a car battery, with two little posts on top and a plus and a minus sign inside it. Some makes color it amber instead, and some show words such as CHECK CHARGING SYSTEM, BATTERY or SERVICE BATTERY CHARGING SYSTEM in the message display. It has nothing to do with the key fob battery message, which usually shows a key symbol.
battery-light.flash: On some cars it flickers or glows dimly at idle and then goes out when you rev the engine or start driving. That points to a charging system that is only just keeping up, usually a slipping drive belt or an alternator on the way out, and it should be tested before it fails completely.

diy.t: Look at the battery terminals
diy.how: With the engine off, open the hood and look at the two cable ends clamped to the battery posts. White, green or blue crusty powder around them, or a clamp that moves when you wiggle it by hand, can stop the battery charging properly. Note what you see and have a shop clean and tighten them, as loosening a battery cable yourself can set off warning lights and radio codes.

diy.t: Check the drive belt at the front of the engine
diy.how: With the engine off and cool, look at the wide ribbed rubber belt that loops around the pulleys at the front of the engine. If it is missing, hanging loose, shredded at the edges or shiny and glazed, the alternator is not being turned and that alone explains the light. Keep your hands clear of the belt and pulleys and just look.

diy.t: Watch your lights and dash at idle
diy.how: Sit in the car with it parked and the engine running and the gear selector in Park or Neutral, then switch the headlights on. If the headlights and dash lights visibly dim, or the dash flickers, the alternator is not producing enough to run the car. Tell the shop whether it got worse with the heater fan or air conditioning on.

diy.t: Get a battery and charging test
diy.how: Many chain auto parts stores can test your battery and alternator, and it takes only a few minutes. Don't drive there with the light on: have the car brought to them, or ask whether they can test it where it sits. The printout tells you whether the battery, the alternator or neither is at fault.

dont: Don't keep driving to see whether the light goes away; the engine can stall anywhere once the battery runs down.
Don't drive it at night or in bad weather if you can avoid it, because the headlights, wipers and defroster all die when the battery runs out.
Don't assume a new battery fixes it; a dead alternator will flatten a brand new battery in a day.
Don't ignore it because the car still starts fine, as the engine can stall anywhere once the charge runs out.

causes2.name: Failing alternator
causes2.tell: Headlights and dash dim at idle, the radio or power windows act strangely, and the battery goes flat again after a jump start. A shop sees low charging voltage at the battery with the engine running, and codes like P0562 for low system voltage often store.
causes2.fix: The alternator is replaced, and the shop checks the belt and the big cable to it at the same time. Many shops also test the new charging output before handing the car back.

causes2.name: Worn-out battery
causes2.tell: The car cranks slowly or needs a jump on cold mornings, and the battery is more than three or four years old. A load test at the shop or parts store shows it failing even though the alternator charges normally.
causes2.fix: The battery is replaced with the correct size and rating, the terminals cleaned, and on many newer cars the new battery is registered to the car's computer so the charging system treats it as new.

causes2.name: Broken or slipping drive belt
causes2.tell: Often a squeal or chirp from the front of the engine, and usually the power steering goes heavy and the heater stops blowing warm at the same time because the belt drives those too. If the belt snapped, the engine temperature will start climbing as well.
causes2.fix: The belt is replaced, and the tensioner and idler pulleys are checked or replaced, since a worn tensioner is what let the belt slip in the first place.

causes2.name: Loose or corroded battery cables
causes2.tell: Crusty buildup on the terminals, a clamp that moves by hand, or a car that behaves normally one minute and cuts out the next. The shop measures a voltage drop across the cable end even though the alternator itself tests fine.
causes2.fix: The terminals are cleaned and tightened, or a corroded cable end or battery cable is replaced.

causes2.name: Charging control or wiring fault
causes2.tell: Everything tests good on its own but the voltage is still wrong, or the light comes and goes. Common on cars where the engine computer controls the alternator output, with codes such as P0620 or P0622 for the generator control circuit.
causes2.fix: The shop traces the circuit between the alternator, the fuse box and the engine computer and repairs the broken wire, connector, fuse or control module it finds.

battery-light.shop: They start with a battery and charging system test, which takes only a few minutes: load-test the battery, then measure the charging voltage at idle and with the headlights and heater fan on. Next they look at the drive belt and tensioner, check the big alternator cable and ground straps for voltage drop, and scan for charging system codes. Half an hour to an hour covers most of it. An intermittent light can take longer because they have to catch it misbehaving.

reset.how: There is nothing to reset here. This light is wired to the actual charging voltage, so it goes out by itself the moment the system charges properly again and stays on as long as it does not. Clearing codes with a scan tool does not repair anything, and the light comes straight back as soon as the engine is running.
reset.note: On many cars built in the last ten years a new battery has to be registered to the car's computer, which is a separate step from resetting a light.

faqs.q: Will a jump start fix the battery light?
faqs.a: No. A jump gets the engine running, but if the alternator or belt is the problem the car is living on whatever charge is left in the battery and can stall again without warning. Have the charging system tested before you rely on the car.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the battery light on?
faqs.a: Not far. Turn off everything you don't need (A/C, radio, seat heaters). Drive only as far as a safe place off the road, not a long trip. If the temperature gauge climbs or the steering gets heavy, stop and turn the engine off. Your owner's manual may say what your car needs; follow it. The car may be running on battery power alone and can stall, which makes the steering and brakes much heavier.

faqs.q: Is it the battery or the alternator?
faqs.a: A battery problem usually shows up as slow or no cranking when you start the car, while an alternator problem shows up once it is running, with dimming lights and this warning. A charging test at a parts store sorts it out in minutes and tells you which part to buy.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the battery light on?
faqs.a: In states that inspect the dashboard, a lit charging warning is a fail. In emissions states the bigger issue is that low system voltage can stop the car's self-tests from finishing, so the computer is not ready to be tested at all.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive at night with this light on?
faqs.a: It is the worst time to try. Headlights, wipers and the defroster draw the most power, so the battery runs down fastest, and when it goes you lose your lights as well as the engine. If it comes on after dark, get off the road and arrange a ride or a tow.

blind-spot-light.look: Usually an amber message in the driver display rather than a symbol: Blind Spot Monitor Unavailable, BSM with a line through it, Service side detection system, or BLIS. Where there is a picture it is two cars seen from above with little waves between them, sometimes inside a mirror shape. Toyota, Honda, Ford, Nissan and Mazda all word it differently.
blind-spot-light.flash: The small amber light in the door mirror flashing while you signal is the system working normally, warning you about a car alongside. That is not a fault. The fault warning is a steady light or a written message in the dash.

diy.t: Wash the back corners of the bumper
diy.how: The radars sit behind the plastic at the rear corners, usually just ahead of the tail lights. With a bucket of warm soapy water and a soft cloth, wipe both corners clean of mud, slush, salt and bugs, and pick off any packed ice or snow by hand. Keep a pressure washer well back; a tight jet can push water in and shift the sensor's aim.

diy.t: Check it has not been switched off in the menu
diy.how: With the car parked, go into the dash or touchscreen settings and look for driver assistance, safety systems, or something named blind spot. If the switch is off, turn it on. Plenty of cars show a warning simply because the feature was turned off, by a previous driver, a valet or a stray tap on the screen.

diy.t: Look over the back end for damage
diy.how: Walk around the back of the parked car and look closely at the bumper corners for cracks, scuffs, dents, or a panel sitting slightly crooked. A low-speed parking knock can crack the bracket or unplug the sensor behind plastic that still looks fine. Also note anything hanging off the back: a bike rack, a trailer or a towed load can block the sensors.

diy.t: Drive a few miles, then restart
diy.how: Once the bumper is clean and dry, drive five or ten minutes on an open road, then switch the car off and start it again. The system rechecks itself as you drive and clears a temporary message on its own. If the warning is back at the next start, or never leaves, it is a real fault and needs a scan tool.

dont: Don't trust the mirror blind spot alerts while this warning is showing; the system is not watching for you.
Don't hold a pressure washer close to the rear bumper corners, as water and a hard jet can knock the sensors out.
Don't take the car back from a body shop after rear bumper work without asking if the blind spot sensors were recalibrated.
Don't keep clearing the message with a code reader and call it fixed; a damaged or misaimed sensor brings it straight back.

causes2.name: Sensors covered in dirt, snow, ice or road salt
causes2.tell: It appeared in bad weather or after a dirty or salty drive, the wording usually says temporarily unavailable, and it clears after a wash and a few miles. By far the most common reason, especially in winter.
causes2.fix: Clean the rear bumper corners and let the system recheck itself as you drive.

causes2.name: Sensor aim knocked off, or never recalibrated after body work
causes2.tell: It started right after a parking bump, a rear bumper repair or replacement, a hitch install or rear suspension work. The warning is steady rather than coming and going, and the bumper is clean.
causes2.fix: A shop refits the sensor square in its bracket and recalibrates it, which needs targets or a road procedure set by the maker. Bodywork and collision shops do this as a matter of course on later cars.

causes2.name: Failed blind spot radar sensor
causes2.tell: A scan names the left or right rear sensor, one side never lights up even with a car clearly beside you, and the bumper looks undamaged. Older cars and ones that live on salted roads get this.
causes2.fix: The bumper cover comes off, that one radar sensor is replaced, and the new one is calibrated.

causes2.name: Wiring, connector or water damage at the bumper
causes2.tell: It comes and goes, works some days and not others, and the codes talk about losing communication with a sensor. Often follows a trailer wiring install, a few salty winters, or water sitting in the bumper.
causes2.fix: The shop traces the harness, cleans or replaces the corroded connector or the damaged section of wire, and seals it so water stays out.

causes2.name: Control module fault or software that needs updating
causes2.tell: Both sides are dead, the message is there at every start, and the scan shows the module not responding or flagging itself. Some makes have a known software update for exactly this complaint.
causes2.fix: The module is reflashed with the current software, or replaced and then coded and calibrated to the car. If a service bulletin covers it and the car is under warranty, the repair may be covered.

blind-spot-light.shop: They start by looking at the back of the car and reading the codes with a scan tool that talks to the body and driver-assist modules, not an engine-only reader. Then they check both rear sensors for power and for whether they are reporting, and look at the bumper for damage, a hitch, or an aftermarket accessory in the way. That is usually about an hour. If the car needs the sensors aimed again, it goes on a calibration setup with targets, which takes longer.

reset.how: This is not a light you are meant to reset. When the cause is simply a blocked sensor, the car clears the message itself once the bumper is clean, usually inside a mile or two of driving. When a sensor is broken, misaimed or unplugged, clearing the code with a scanner changes nothing: the warning returns at the next start or the next time you move. Fix the sensor, the wiring or the aim and the message goes away on its own.
reset.note: After a sensor is replaced or a bumper repaired, most makes need a calibration procedure before the system will work again; a code clear is not a substitute.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the blind spot warning on?
faqs.a: In most places, yes. Blind spot monitoring is a convenience and safety extra, not part of an emissions test, and state safety checks look at brakes, lights, tires and steering. Rules differ by state, so if you are unsure, ask your inspection station before you go.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive at night or on the highway with it on?
faqs.a: The car itself is fine, and nothing about braking or steering changes. The risk is habit: if you have got used to the mirror lights, you may change lanes without really looking. Set your mirrors properly and turn your head before every lane change until it is fixed.

faqs.q: Why did it come on in the rain and then go away?
faqs.a: Spray, slush and packed snow sit on the bumper and blind the radar, so the car shuts the system down and says it is unavailable for now. Once the muck is gone and you have driven a few minutes it checks itself again and the message clears. If it keeps happening in dry weather, something is actually wrong.

faqs.q: Did my bumper repair break the blind spot monitor?
faqs.a: It can. The sensors live behind the rear bumper corners, and taking the cover off, straightening the body or changing the rear ride height can move them out of aim. They often need a calibration afterwards. Go back to the shop that did the work and ask whether that step was done.

faqs.q: Can I just clear the code with a cheap scanner?
faqs.a: You can clear it, but it is not a repair. If the sensor is damaged, dirty or out of aim, the warning comes straight back.

brake-pad-wear-light.look: An amber circle standing for the brake disc, with short broken or dashed lines curving away from each side for the pads, sometimes with an exclamation mark inside. It looks much like the red brake system light, but that one has solid curved lines and is far more urgent. Many European cars show words instead, such as Brake pad wear or Check brake pads.

diy.t: Look at the pads through the wheel
diy.how: Wait until the car has been parked at least 30 minutes; brake parts get hot enough to burn. Stand beside the parked car and look through the gaps in the wheel at the shiny disc. You will see the pad squeezed against it inside a metal bracket. What you are judging is the thickness of the dark friction block, ignoring the steel backing plate behind it. Anything thinner than about 1/8 inch (3 mm), roughly two stacked quarters, is finished. Do all four wheels, turning the steering to full lock first to see the front ones better.

diy.t: Listen to what the brakes are telling you
diy.how: Drive gently somewhere quiet with the windows down and brake a few times. A high pitched squeal as you slow down is the built in wear tab doing its job and matches the light. A deep grinding or scraping, or a noise you can feel through the pedal, means the material is gone and steel is cutting the disc. In that case stop driving it.

diy.t: Check the brake fluid level
diy.how: With the car parked and cool, find the small reservoir with a brake symbol on the cap, usually at the back of the engine bay on the driver's side, and read the level against the markings on the side without opening it. Worn pads make the level sit slightly lower than normal. A level well below the minimum points at a leak instead, which is a different and much more serious problem.

diy.t: Compare one corner against the others
diy.how: Look at the pad thickness at every wheel and note any corner that is much worse than the rest. After a normal drive, hold the back of your hand near each wheel without touching it; one that throws off noticeably more heat than the others suggests a brake that is dragging. Tell the shop which corner it was, because that changes the repair from pads to a caliper.

diy.t: Read the service menu on European cars
diy.how: BMW, Mercedes, Volvo, Audi and some others show remaining brake pad life in the driver information menu, often as a mileage or a bar graph. Scroll through with the steering wheel buttons until you find the brake or service entry. It gives you a real number to work with instead of guessing from the light.

dont: Don't ignore grinding or scraping; that is steel cutting into the disc and it makes the car stop worse.
Don't just clear the message and move on. Pads do not get thicker because a warning was dismissed.
Don't have pads done on one wheel only. Both wheels on an axle are always replaced together.
Don't tow, carry heavy loads or take long downhill runs while this light is on.

causes2.name: Brake pads worn out from normal use
causes2.tell: Material visible through the wheel is down to a thin sliver, there is often a squeal when braking, and the mileage since the last brake job is high. Fronts usually wear out first because they do most of the stopping. This is the reason nearly every time.
causes2.fix: New pads and a new wear sensor on that axle, with the caliper slide pins cleaned and greased and the brake fluid topped off. Figures below are for one axle, front or rear.

causes2.name: Pads and discs both worn out
causes2.tell: Very common once the warning has been on a while, or if there was any grinding. The disc face feels ridged or has a lip you can catch a fingernail on, and there may be a pulse through the pedal when you slow down.
causes2.fix: New pads, discs and wear sensor on that axle. Modern discs are usually replaced rather than machined. Again this is per axle, and trucks and performance cars sit at the top of the range.

causes2.name: Wear sensor damaged or never replaced
causes2.tell: The pads measure healthy but the light is on, or the warning appeared right after a brake job. The sensor is a thin wire looped into the pad, and it is easy to tear or leave unplugged. Sometimes the connector is simply hanging loose.
causes2.fix: Fit a new wear sensor, or repair and reconnect the plug.

causes2.name: Sticking caliper or seized slide pins
causes2.tell: One corner is worn far more than the rest, that wheel runs hotter than the others after a drive, and the car may pull slightly or feel like it is dragging. Fuel economy often drops and there can be a smell after a long run.
causes2.fix: Free off or replace the caliper, clean and grease the slide pins or fit a new bracket, then new pads and usually a new disc on that side because of the uneven wear.

causes2.name: Wiring or connector fault in the sensor circuit
causes2.tell: The warning comes and goes, or shows up after work near the suspension or after driving through deep water or road salt. The pads look fine and the sensor itself is intact, but the wire running up to the car is chafed or green with corrosion.
causes2.fix: Trace and repair the wire or replace the connector and pigtail.

brake-pad-wear-light.shop: The shop takes the wheels off and measures what is left of the friction material on every pad with a gauge, and compares it with the maker's limit; most shops recommend new pads at about 1/8 inch (3 mm). They measure the discs for thickness and for warping, check that the calipers and slide pins move freely, and look at how evenly each pad has worn, because one odd corner changes the diagnosis. If the pads turn out to be fine they test the sensor and its wiring. A brake inspection like this is normally about half an hour, and many shops fold the charge into the repair.

reset.how: There is nothing to reset in the usual sense. The light is reporting the actual thickness of your brake pads, and clearing the message does not add material back; it returns as soon as the car checks the sensor again, often within a mile. The only real reset comes after the pads and the sensor have genuinely been replaced: on BMW, Mercedes, Volvo and some other makes the brake service indicator then has to be reset through the dash menu or with a scan tool before the message clears for good. On most Japanese and American cars it simply goes out by itself once a new sensor is fitted.
reset.note: If the warning switches itself off while the pads are still thin, suspect a broken sensor wire rather than good news.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the brake pad wear light on?
faqs.a: Usually a few hundred miles of ordinary driving, because the sensor triggers with a little material still left. Treat it as a reason to book the work this week, not this month. The moment you hear grinding, that window has closed and the car should not be driven.

faqs.q: Is the brake pad wear light the same as the red brake warning light?
faqs.a: No. This amber one means the pads are worn and the brakes still work normally. A red brake light means the parking brake is on or the brake system itself has a problem, most often low fluid from a leak, and that one means do not drive the car until it is checked.

faqs.q: Will a brake pad warning light fail an inspection?
faqs.a: The light itself is not usually what fails you, but in states with a safety inspection the inspector measures pad thickness, and pads worn to the warning point will often fail. Grooved or undersized discs fail as well.

faqs.q: Why is the light still on after I put new brake pads in?
faqs.a: Almost always one of two things: the old wear sensor was reused or left unplugged, or the car needs its brake service indicator reset through the dash. The sensor is a one-use item on most cars, so it goes in with every set of pads.

faqs.q: The brakes squeal but no light came on. Does that mean anything?
faqs.a: Yes, it often means exactly the same thing. Many cars have no pad warning light and use a small metal tab on the pad that scrapes the disc to make a squeal when the material gets low. If the squeal happens whenever you brake and goes quiet when you let off, have the pads measured.

brake-warning-light.look: A red light in the middle of the instrument cluster: an exclamation point inside a circle, with a curved bracket on each side. Some makes spell out BRAKE in red letters instead, and many add a separate amber P in a circle just for the parking brake. Newer cars may show a written message such as Brake fluid low or Brake system fault in the driver display.

diy.t: Make sure the parking brake is all the way off
diy.how: Push the lever fully down, or lift the foot pedal all the way up, or press the electric parking brake switch once and look for the word PARK or a P to go out. Pull it on and release it again, firmly, then look at the light. On a lot of cars this one step is the whole problem.

diy.t: Look at the brake fluid level
diy.how: With the engine off and cool, open the hood and find the small see-through plastic tank on the driver's side against the firewall, usually marked with the same circle-and-exclamation-point symbol. Read the level through the side of the tank without opening the cap. It should sit between the MIN and MAX marks. Near or below MIN is the common reason this light is on.

diy.t: Look for leaking fluid
diy.how: Walk around the parked car and look at the ground where it has been sitting for wet patches. Then look at the inner face of each wheel and the back of each tire for wet streaks or dried runs. Brake fluid is clear to light brown and feels slightly oily. Any sign of it means a leak, and a leak means the brakes can run out of pressure.

diy.t: Feel the pedal while parked
diy.how: With the car parked, the engine off and the transmission in Park, press the brake pedal and hold steady pressure on it for about fifteen seconds. It should stop firm and stay put. If it slowly sinks toward the floor, or feels spongy, do not drive the car anywhere. Call for a tow instead.

diy.t: Check what your car's manual says this light means
diy.how: Look up the red brake symbol in the warning lights section of the owner's manual, for your model and year. Some cars use this one light for the parking brake, low fluid and an electronic brake fault all at once, and the manual tells you which combination of lights and chimes goes with which.

dont: Don't keep driving to see if it clears. This light can mean the brakes are losing fluid, and that gets worse, not better.
Don't just top the fluid up and move on. Brake fluid does not evaporate, so if it is low, something used it or something is leaking.
Don't pour in anything but the fluid type printed on the reservoir cap, usually DOT 3 or DOT 4. The wrong fluid damages seals.
Don't drive it if the pedal sinks or feels soft. Have it towed; that is the one symptom that most often ends in no brakes at all.

causes2.name: Parking brake still partly on, or a stuck parking brake switch
causes2.tell: The light goes out, or flickers, when you pull the parking brake on and release it again. Everything else is normal: the pedal is firm, the fluid is full, and the car stops the way it always has. On older cars the little switch at the base of the lever sticks and reports the brake as on when it isn't.
causes2.fix: A shop adjusts the parking brake cable or replaces the switch at the lever or pedal. It is a small job on most cars.

causes2.name: Low brake fluid because the brake pads are worn out
causes2.tell: Fluid sits at or below the MIN mark, and the brakes squeal, grind or feel like they need a longer push. Looking through the wheel spokes, the pad pressed against the shiny disc looks thin, like a coin rather than a finger's width. As pads wear, fluid moves out of the tank to fill the gap, so the level drops on its own.
causes2.fix: New brake pads, and new discs if they are grooved or too thin, then the fluid is brought back to level. Usually quoted one axle at a time, front or rear.

causes2.name: A brake fluid leak at a line, hose or caliper
causes2.tell: The level keeps dropping after you top it up, there are wet streaks or drips near one wheel, and the pedal may travel further than it used to. Steel lines rust through underneath in salt states; rubber hoses split; the caliper, the clamp that squeezes the disc, can weep from its seal.
causes2.fix: The rusted line, split hose or leaking caliper is replaced, and then the system is bled so there is no air left in it.

causes2.name: Failing brake master cylinder
causes2.tell: Hold your foot on the pedal and it sinks slowly toward the floor, yet there is no puddle and nothing wet at the wheels, because the fluid is leaking past seals inside the part itself. The pedal often feels fine for the first inch and vague after that. The red light may come on alongside the amber ABS light.
causes2.fix: The master cylinder, the pump the brake pedal pushes on, is replaced and the whole system bled.

causes2.name: Faulty brake fluid level sensor or its wiring
causes2.tell: The fluid is clearly full between the marks, the pedal is firm, and nothing is leaking, but the light stays on anyway, or comes and goes over bumps. Unplugging and reseating the small connector on top of the fluid tank sometimes makes it flicker, which points at the sensor rather than the brakes.
causes2.fix: The level sensor, which is usually built into the reservoir cap or the side of the tank, is replaced, or a broken wire to it is repaired.

brake-warning-light.shop: A shop starts by releasing the parking brake and looking at the fluid level and its color, then plugs a scan tool into the brake and ABS computers to read any stored codes. They measure how much pad and disc is left at each wheel, look along the brake lines and hoses for wet spots or rust, and press the pedal to see whether it holds or sinks. A short road test confirms it. That first look usually takes half an hour to an hour; tracing a slow leak takes longer.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a service reminder, so there is nothing to reset. Pulling a fuse, disconnecting the battery or clearing the code with a scan tool only turns the bulb off for a moment, and the car runs its own brake check every time you start it, so the light comes straight back while the fault is still there. Fix the cause, whether that is the parking brake, the fluid, the pads or a leak, and the light goes out by itself.
reset.note: A few cars store a hard brake fault that a scan tool has to clear once the repair is done, so the light may need one visit to go out.

faqs.q: Can I drive with the red brake light on?
faqs.a: Only after you have proved it is the parking brake. Release the parking brake fully; if the light goes out, drive on. If it stays on, treat the car as unsafe until someone checks the fluid and the pedal, because this light also means the brakes may be losing the pressure they need to stop you.

faqs.q: My brake light is on but the brakes feel completely normal. Why?
faqs.a: The usual answers are a parking brake that is not fully released, a fluid level that has crept just below the sensor as the pads wear, or a bad level sensor. Brakes can feel normal right up until they don't, so it is still worth checking the fluid and the pad thickness rather than waiting.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the brake warning light on?
faqs.a: In states that do a safety inspection, a lit red brake warning light is a standard fail, and so is a brake fluid leak or pads worn past the limit. Rules differ by state, so check your own state's inspection list, but plan on fixing it first.

faqs.q: Does the brake warning light reset itself?
faqs.a: Yes, once the real problem is gone. Release a stuck parking brake or bring the fluid back to level and the light usually goes out within a few seconds or on the next start. If it goes out and then returns, the fault is still there and the car is finding it again.

faqs.q: Can I just add brake fluid myself?
faqs.a: If the red BRAKE light stays on after you fully release the parking brake, pull over as soon as it's safe and arrange a tow. A soft pedal, a pedal that slowly sinks under steady pressure, or leaking brake fluid are also reasons to stop driving. Adding fluid won't repair a leak or make the brakes safe to use.

def-light.look: A small amber light or dash message usually low in the instrument cluster, often shown as a tank or canister with the letters DEF on it and a drip above. Many trucks show no symbol at all and instead spell out a message such as DEF Low Refill Soon, Service DEF System, or Incorrect DEF Detected. European diesels call the same fluid AdBlue, so the message may say AdBlue instead of DEF.
def-light.flash: On some trucks and cars the light stops being steady and starts flashing, or the message changes to a mileage countdown, when the tank is nearly empty or the system has a fault. Treat a flashing light or a countdown as urgent: once the countdown runs out the vehicle will limit itself to a crawl.

diy.t: Read the exact wording on the dash
diy.how: There is a big difference between a message that says the fluid is low and one that says service the system. A low or refill message means you just need to add fluid. A service, fault, or incorrect fluid message means a part or the fluid itself is the problem and adding more will not clear it. Write the message down word for word, plus any mileage number it shows, before you do anything else.

diy.t: Check how much fluid is in the tank
diy.how: Most diesels show a diesel exhaust fluid level in the driver information menu, in the same place you find trip and fuel economy screens. Scroll through the menus with the steering wheel buttons while the vehicle is parked and switched on. If your vehicle has no gauge, the owner's manual will tell you where the tank is and how much it holds.

diy.t: Top the tank up with fresh DEF
diy.how: Diesel exhaust fluid is sold in jugs at gas stations and parts stores. The filler is a small cap, usually blue, next to the diesel filler or under the hood. Add at least two gallons, because a tiny splash is often not enough for the vehicle to notice. Put nothing else in that tank: no diesel, no water, no washer fluid. The warning normally goes out after you restart and drive a short distance.
diy.tools: A jug of DEF with a spout

diy.t: Check the fluid before you pour it in
diy.how: Diesel exhaust fluid goes bad with age and heat. Look for a date on the jug and skip anything more than about a year old or any jug that has been sitting in a hot shed or truck bed all summer. It should be clear and water thin with no cloudiness or bits in it. Bad fluid is a common reason for an incorrect fluid message.

diy.t: Look for white crust around the cap and filler
diy.how: With the engine off and cool, look at the filler neck and cap area and anywhere you can plainly see the fluid lines. Dried diesel exhaust fluid leaves a white, crusty, salt like deposit. Crust usually means a spill or a slow leak, and crust is worth telling the shop about because the same deposits also block the part that sprays the fluid into the exhaust. Wipe spills with a wet rag and plain water.

dont: Don't ignore a mileage countdown. When it runs out most diesels cut the top speed to a walking pace and you may need a tow.
Don't pour anything but diesel exhaust fluid into that tank. Diesel, water or washer fluid in there turns a refill into a tank and pump job.
Don't buy or keep DEF that has been baking in the heat or has been open a long time. Old fluid sets off fault messages.
Don't let anyone 'delete' or switch off the emissions system to make the light go away. It is illegal on a road vehicle and it ruins resale.

causes2.name: Tank is simply low on fluid
causes2.tell: The message says the fluid is low or asks you to refill, the level gauge in the dash menu reads near empty, and there is no stored fault for a part. This is the most common reason by far, especially after towing or a long highway trip, because the engine uses more fluid when it works hard.
causes2.fix: Buy diesel exhaust fluid and pour it in yourself. Add at least two gallons so the vehicle sees a real change in level.

causes2.name: Wrong, contaminated or stale fluid in the tank
causes2.tell: The dash says something like incorrect fluid detected, or the warning came back soon after a refill with old or low-quality fluid. It also shows up after someone has topped the tank with the wrong liquid by mistake, or after the tank has been open to dirt and water.
causes2.fix: A shop drains and flushes the tank and refills it with fresh fluid, then clears the fault. If the wrong liquid went in, the pump and lines may have to come out too.

causes2.name: Blocked fluid injector (the nozzle that sprays into the exhaust)
causes2.tell: White crystal deposits at the nozzle or its plug, fluid use that suddenly changes, and stored codes about the reductant injector or poor exhaust cleaning. A check engine light often comes on with it.
causes2.fix: The nozzle comes out, gets cleaned if the deposits are only on the tip and it passes an electrical test, and gets replaced if it is cracked, shorted or clogged inside.

causes2.name: Failed NOx sensor
causes2.tell: Codes about exhaust cleaning efficiency or the NOx sensor circuit, with a tank that is full and fluid that is good. This one can look exactly like a fluid problem because the sensor is what tells the computer whether the fluid is doing its job.
causes2.fix: The faulty sensor is replaced. There are usually two, one before and one after the exhaust cleaning unit, so the shop has to confirm which one is bad.

causes2.name: Fluid pump or tank header unit failure (pump, heater and level sensor)
causes2.tell: Codes about fluid pressure being too low or too high, a heater circuit fault that shows up in cold weather, or a level reading that is stuck or jumps around even though the tank has fluid in it. Often the dash says to service the system with a mileage countdown.
causes2.fix: The pump or the whole header assembly on top of the tank is replaced.

def-light.shop: A shop starts by reading the stored codes and looking at live data: tank level, fluid pressure, heater and sensor readings, and whether the exhaust cleaning system is working. Then they check the fluid itself with a refractometer, look for white crystal deposits and leaks, and test the pump and the spray nozzle. A straightforward low level or bad fluid check takes well under an hour. Chasing a pump, heater or sensor fault usually takes one to two hours because the system has to be run up to pressure and watched.

reset.how: A low fluid warning is meant to clear itself. Add at least two gallons of fresh fluid, switch the vehicle off, restart it and drive a few minutes so the sensor reads the new level. Most vehicles drop the message on their own at that point. A fault or incorrect fluid message is different: it will not clear by refilling, and clearing the code with a scan tool only hides it until the vehicle tests the system again. Once the vehicle has reached the crawling speed limit stage, many makes will not lift it until a shop resets the system with a scan tool after the repair.
reset.note: The exact number of gallons needed and how far you must drive before the message clears vary by make, model and year.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the DEF light on?
faqs.a: While the message only says the fluid is low you normally have a few hundred miles of ordinary driving. Once the dash starts counting down miles, you are on a clock: when it reaches zero most diesels cut the top speed to a walking pace, which can leave you stranded. Fill it before the countdown gets low rather than after.

faqs.q: Will my truck really stop running if I run out of DEF?
faqs.a: It will not blow up, but it will stop being usable. Pickups typically limit the top speed to about five miles an hour once the countdown ends and the engine is shut off, restarted, idled a long time or refueled. Many European diesel cars go further and refuse to restart at all until fluid is added.

faqs.q: Can I just add DEF myself?
faqs.a: Yes. It is one of the few things on a modern diesel that is genuinely a do it yourself job. The fluid is sold in sealed jugs with a spout, the filler cap is usually blue and right next to the diesel filler, and nothing is hot or under pressure. Just make sure the jug says diesel exhaust fluid and nothing else goes in that hole.

faqs.q: Will it pass inspection with the DEF light on?
faqs.a: In states with an emissions test, a lit warning for the exhaust cleaning system or a stored emissions fault is a fail. A simple low level warning often clears once you refill and drive, which is enough to pass. A system fault has to be repaired first, because the test reads the vehicle's own self checks.

faqs.q: Does the DEF light reset itself after I fill the tank?
faqs.a: Usually yes, within a few minutes of driving, as long as you added enough fluid, at least two gallons. If the light stays on after a refill and a short drive, the vehicle is telling you something other than the level is wrong, and that part needs a shop with a scan tool.

door-open-light.look: A red or amber outline of a car seen from above with one or two doors swung open, shown in the cluster or on the main screen. Many newer cars draw the whole car and highlight only the door that is open, and some show words instead, such as Door Open, Door Ajar or Driver Door Open. The hood and trunk versions use the same car outline with the hood or the trunk lid raised.

diy.t: Open and firmly re-close each door
diy.how: With the car parked, open one door at a time and push it shut properly, listening for the second click. Watch the dash as you do it, because the light usually goes out on the door that was the problem. Include the trunk, the hood and, on some cars, the fuel filler flap and the rear tailgate glass.

diy.t: See which door the dash is reporting
diy.how: Look at the car picture in the cluster or scroll the dash menu to the warnings page. Most cars after about 2010 will tell you which door, hood or trunk they think is open. If it names a door you never use, such as a rear door, that is almost always a worn switch rather than a door left ajar.

diy.t: Clean the latch and the door frame
diy.how: Open the suspect door and look at the metal latch in the edge of the door and the small rubber covered button or plunger in the door frame. Wipe away road dirt, leaves, pet hair or ice with a cloth. Dirt and frozen water are a very common reason a door reads as open when it is shut.

diy.t: Spray the latch with lubricant
diy.how: With the door open and the engine off, aim a little silicone or white lithium spray into the moving part of the latch in the door edge, then open and close the door several times to work it in. A dry, sticky latch often does not travel far enough to tell the car it is shut. Wipe off any overspray so it does not mark your clothes.

diy.t: Check whether the interior lights stay on
diy.how: Lock the car, wait a few minutes and look through the glass. If the interior lights or the courtesy lights are still burning, the car thinks a door is open and your battery is slowly going flat. Turn the interior light switch to the off position as a short term fix, and get the switch repaired soon.

dont: Don't drive off with a door that is only on its first click, even across a parking lot; it can swing open on a turn.
Don't leave the car parked for days with the interior lights stuck on, because it will flatten the battery.
Don't slam the door harder and harder to make the light go out; that bends the latch and the frame.
Don't tape over the switch or pull the bulb to hide it, as the car also uses that signal for the locks and the alarm.

causes2.name: A door, hood, trunk or fuel flap not fully shut
causes2.tell: The light goes out the moment you re-close the right panel, and the dash names that panel. Very common with a rear door shut by a child, a trunk closed gently, or a hood dropped from too low so it rests on the safety catch.
causes2.fix: Nothing to repair. Close the panel properly and make sure the hood drops onto both catches.

causes2.name: Worn or stuck door frame plunger switch
causes2.tell: The warning comes and goes over bumps, or stays on for one named door that is clearly shut, and the interior lights often stay on with it. The small rubber covered button in the door frame feels gritty, sticks in, or does not spring back. Worst in winter and on older cars.
causes2.fix: The switch is unplugged and replaced.

causes2.name: Switch inside the door latch has failed
causes2.tell: On most cars built in the last twenty years the sensor lives inside the latch, so the warning usually arrives alongside other oddities on the same door, such as locks that work only sometimes, an unusual noise when locking, or the alarm going off for no reason.
causes2.fix: The door trim panel comes off and the whole latch or lock actuator unit is replaced, as the switch is not sold separately.

causes2.name: Broken wire in the rubber trunk between door and body
causes2.tell: The warning changes as you move the door part way, or it affects several things on one door at once, such as the window, the mirror and the speaker. The flexible rubber tube at the hinge end has flexed thousands of times and a wire inside has cracked.
causes2.fix: The wiring in the trunk is traced and the broken wire is repaired or the harness section is replaced.

causes2.name: Door out of alignment or a worn striker
causes2.tell: The door needs an extra shove to shut, sits slightly out from the body compared with the other side, or has wind noise at speed. Often follows a minor knock or years of being leaned on. The latch never quite reaches its fully closed position, so the car reports it as open.
causes2.fix: The striker on the body or the hinge position is adjusted so the door closes squarely, and a worn striker is replaced.

door-open-light.shop: The technician looks at the dash first to see which panel the car is reporting, then goes to that latch. With a scan tool they can watch the body computer live and open and close that one door to see whether the signal changes. If it never changes, they unplug the switch or latch and test it directly, and they flex the wiring trunk at the hinge while watching. Most of these are found and confirmed inside half an hour to an hour.

reset.how: There is nothing to reset here. This light is simply the car repeating what the latch switches are telling it, so the moment every panel is properly shut it goes out on its own. If it stays on, clearing it does not fix anything: pulling a fuse or disconnecting the battery may blank it for a moment, but it comes straight back because the switch or wiring is still faulty. The only real fix is repairing the switch, the latch or the wire.
reset.note: A frozen or dirt packed latch can behave the same way, so it is worth cleaning and lubricating before anyone replaces a part.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive with the door ajar light on?
faqs.a: If every door, the hood and the trunk are genuinely shut, the light itself doesn't change how the car drives. If something really is ajar, stop and close it: a door on its first click can swing open on a corner, and a hood that isn't latched can fly up and block your view.

faqs.q: Will a stuck door ajar light drain my battery?
faqs.a: It can, and this is the real reason to fix it. The car thinks a door is open, so the interior lights may stay on and the body computer may never go to sleep. A few days of that is enough to leave you with a car that will not start.

faqs.q: Why is it on when all the doors are closed?
faqs.a: Because the car cannot see the door, only a small switch. If that switch is worn, dirty, frozen or wired through a cracked cable at the hinge, it keeps sending the open signal. Cleaning and lubricating the latch fixes a fair number of these, and the rest need the switch, latch or wiring repaired.

faqs.q: Can it be the hood or the trunk instead of a door?
faqs.a: Yes. Many cars use the same symbol for the hood and the trunk or tailgate, and some include the fuel flap or the rear glass. The hood switch is the one most often caught out by dirt and corrosion, since it sits in the engine bay. Lift and re-close the hood firmly and see if the light clears.

faqs.q: Will it stop my car passing inspection?
faqs.a: A door ajar warning is not part of an emissions test, which looks at the check engine light. A state safety inspection can fail a door or hood that will not latch properly, because that is a genuine safety problem, so get a door that does not close fixed before you go.

dpf-light.look: An amber light in the main instrument cluster, usually drawn as a box or canister shape with dots or specks inside it and a short exhaust pipe at each end. Some makes use a different picture, such as an exhaust pipe with dots puffing out of it, and many newer vehicles skip the symbol and put a message on the screen instead, like Diesel Particulate Filter Full or Exhaust Filter Nearly Full Drive to Clean.
dpf-light.flash: On several makes a flashing or blinking filter light, or the same light paired with a check engine light, means the filter is badly blocked and the vehicle can no longer clean it by itself. At that point driving on the highway will not fix it and you need a shop before the engine goes into reduced power.

diy.t: Take a steady highway drive to let it clean itself
diy.how: This light often just means the filter needs a hot run to burn off its soot. Get the engine fully warmed up, then drive at a steady highway speed for twenty to thirty minutes without stopping, so the engine turns a bit faster (on a manual, one gear lower than normal; on an automatic, just hold a steady speed). Do not switch the engine off partway. If the light goes out during or shortly after the drive, that is exactly what was supposed to happen. Don't park over dry grass or leaves right after: the exhaust runs very hot while the filter cleans itself.

diy.t: Check you have enough fuel first
diy.how: The cleaning cycle burns extra fuel, so most diesels refuse to start one when the tank is low, often below about a quarter full. Look at the fuel gauge before you set off and fill up if it is anywhere near the bottom. A full tank is the simplest reason a long drive sometimes fails to clear the light.

diy.t: Check the engine oil level and when it was last changed
diy.how: With the engine off and cool and the vehicle on level ground, pull the dipstick, wipe it, push it fully back in and read it. The cleaning cycle puts a little diesel into the oil, so oil that is overfull, thin, diesel smelling or long overdue will block the cycle. If the oil is overdue or the level is above the top mark, book an oil change with the correct low ash diesel oil.

diy.t: Note every other light that is on with it
diy.how: The vehicle will not run a cleaning cycle while certain other faults are stored, so the filter light with company tells a very different story to the filter light on its own. Write down whether the check engine light, glow plug light, coolant temperature warning or reduced power message is also showing, and tell the shop. That list often points straight at the real cause.

diy.t: Watch the temperature gauge on your next drive
diy.how: A diesel that never gets properly warm cannot clean its filter. On your next normal drive, watch whether the coolant temperature gauge climbs to its usual middle position within about ten minutes and stays there. If it sits low or drifts back down on the highway, mention it: a stuck thermostat is a common hidden reason the filter keeps filling up.

dont: Don't shut the engine off in the middle of a cleaning cycle if you can avoid it. Interrupted cycles are a main reason the filter never finishes cleaning.
Don't just carry on with short cold trips and hope. Every short trip adds soot the engine never gets hot enough to burn off.
Don't ignore the light until the engine goes into reduced power. Driving to clean the filter is easy; a fully blocked filter is a major repair on a diesel.
Don't have the filter gutted, drilled or 'deleted'. It is illegal on a road vehicle, it fails emissions testing and it destroys the resale value.
Don't park over dry grass, leaves or anything that can burn right after a cleaning drive; the exhaust is very hot.

causes2.name: Too many short, cold trips, so the filter never cleaned itself
causes2.tell: The vehicle is used for school runs, town errands and a short commute, the light came on with no other warnings, and a scan shows the soot level high but nothing broken. This is the ordinary, nothing is wrong reason, and it is the most common one.
causes2.fix: If the soot level is already too high for the vehicle to clean itself, a shop starts a cleaning cycle with a scan tool.

causes2.name: Faulty pressure sensor or its hoses
causes2.tell: The light comes and goes, or it comes back soon after a good highway run, and a scan stores a code about the filter pressure sensor or filter restriction. The small hoses that feed the sensor can also be cracked, soot blocked or pushed off, which makes the vehicle read a blockage that is not there.
causes2.fix: The sensor or its hoses are replaced and the stored fault cleared.

causes2.name: Exhaust temperature sensor fault blocking the cleaning cycle
causes2.tell: The filter light stays on and the vehicle never starts a cleaning cycle at all, however far you drive, and a scan shows an exhaust gas temperature sensor code. These sensors have to agree before the computer will let the cycle run.
causes2.fix: The faulty temperature sensor is replaced.

causes2.name: An engine fault making far too much soot
causes2.tell: The filter light keeps returning after it has been cleaned, often with a check engine light, black smoke, poor economy or a rough idle. Worn or leaking fuel injectors, a stuck exhaust gas recirculation valve or a tired turbo all fill the filter faster than the vehicle can empty it.
causes2.fix: The shop finds and repairs the engine fault first, then cleans or replaces the filter. Fixing the filter without fixing the cause just means doing it again.

causes2.name: Filter is blocked with ash and needs cleaning or replacement
causes2.tell: High mileage, a scan showing the filter near its limit or a failed cleaning cycle, and usually reduced engine power. Ash is the leftover that burning soot cannot remove, so it builds up over the life of the filter and eventually fills it for good.
causes2.fix: The filter comes off and goes into a cleaning oven where heat and pressure strip the ash, or it is replaced. Many car filters are welded into the exhaust, so a dealer will often only offer replacement.

dpf-light.shop: A shop plugs in a scan tool and looks at the real numbers first: how full of soot the filter is, the pressure sensor reading, how far you have driven since the last cleaning cycle, and whether any other fault is blocking a cycle. If the filter is not too far gone they start a cleaning cycle themselves, either parked or on a road test, and watch the exhaust temperature climb. Reading the data and deciding takes under an hour; the cleaning cycle itself adds roughly thirty to forty five minutes of running.

reset.how: This light is meant to go out by itself once the filter has been cleaned, either by a long hot drive or by a cleaning cycle a shop starts with a scan tool. If a shop cleans or replaces the filter, part of the job is resetting the soot and ash counters so the vehicle starts counting from zero again. What does not work is clearing the code to make the light go away: the filter is still full, the vehicle measures it again within a few miles and the light comes straight back, usually with more soot in there than before.
reset.note: How full the filter can get before the vehicle refuses to clean it on its own, and whether a parked cleaning cycle is even allowed, differ by make and model.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the DPF light on?
faqs.a: If it is the only light on, you can drive, and driving is actually the fix. Deal with it in the next day or two rather than the next month. Keep going on short trips for weeks and the filter fills past the point where the vehicle can clean itself, and then it needs a shop.

faqs.q: What speed and how long do I need to drive to clear it?
faqs.a: Get the engine fully warm, then hold a steady highway speed, roughly fifty to sixty five miles an hour, for twenty to thirty minutes without stopping. Using a lower gear so the engine turns faster helps it get hot enough. If two of those drives do nothing, stop trying and have it scanned.

faqs.q: The light went out on its own. Was something wrong?
faqs.a: Probably not. Going out on its own means the cleaning cycle finished, which is the system working as designed. If it keeps coming back every few hundred miles, though, that is a sign something is filling the filter faster than normal and it is worth a scan.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the DPF light on?
faqs.a: In a state with an emissions test, no. The test reads the vehicle's own self checks, and a lit filter warning or a stored filter fault is a fail. If a good highway drive clears the light and no fault stays stored, it can pass, but a vehicle that needs the filter cleaned or replaced has to be fixed first.

faqs.q: Do those DPF cleaner bottles you pour in the tank work?
faqs.a: They can help a filter that is only mildly loaded, mostly by helping the soot burn at a lower temperature, so they are worth a try alongside a highway drive. They will not unblock a filter that is already full or packed with ash, and they do nothing at all for a bad sensor or an engine fault.

engine-temperature-light.look: It sits in the main instrument cluster and looks like a thermometer dipped in liquid, with wavy lines under it. Red means too hot; on many cars the same symbol glows blue for a minute after a cold start, which only means the engine is still warming up. Some makes show words instead, such as ENGINE HOT or COOLANT TEMP, and some just swing the temperature needle into the red band.
engine-temperature-light.flash: On some European cars a blinking coolant symbol means low coolant and a steady one means the engine is too hot, but makes differ and a flashing red light can also mean overheating. Either way, pull over when it's safe, turn the engine off, and check the owner's manual for what your car's light means.

diy.t: Let it cool, then check the coolant tank level
diy.how: Wait at least half an hour after shutting the engine off, until the hood is cool to the touch. Find the translucent plastic coolant tank in the engine bay and look at the level against the MIN and MAX marks on its side. Do not open the black or metal cap on the radiator or the tank while anything is warm, because the system is under pressure and the liquid is scalding.

diy.t: Look for a leak on the ground and in the engine bay
diy.how: With the car parked and cool, look at the ground near the front wheels and the middle of the engine bay for a wet patch. Coolant is usually bright green, orange, pink or blue and feels slippery, and it smells faintly sweet. Also look for dried crusty streaks on hoses and around the radiator, which show where it has been seeping.

diy.t: Check the front of the car for blocked airflow
diy.how: Look through the grille at the radiator from the front of the car. Leaves, a plastic bag, road debris or a thick layer of bugs across the face of it will stop air passing through and make the engine run hot, especially in slow traffic. Pull off anything loose by hand with the engine off and cold.

diy.t: Read the temperature gauge and the manual page
diy.how: If your dash has a temperature gauge, note where the needle sits when the warning appears and whether it climbs in traffic or at highway speed. Then look up the coolant warning in your owner's manual, which tells you exactly what your car means by that light. Both details save the shop guessing time later.

dont: Don't keep driving to 'see if it clears' with the red temperature light on, even for a few miles.
Don't open the radiator or coolant cap while the engine is warm; pressurised coolant can spray out and scald you.
Don't pour cold water into a hot engine, as the sudden shock can crack the head or block.
Don't restart and keep running the engine just to move the car further than the nearest safe spot.

causes2.name: Low coolant from a leaking hose, clamp or tank
causes2.tell: The tank is below the MIN mark, and there is a wet or crusty trail on a hose end, a clamp or the plastic tank itself. The light often comes on in stages, hotter in traffic first. No stored code in many cases, or P0128 if the engine never reaches proper temperature.
causes2.fix: The shop pressure-tests the cooling system to find the leak, replaces the split hose, clamp or cracked tank, then refills and bleeds the air out of the system.

causes2.name: Thermostat stuck closed
causes2.tell: The engine heats up fast, within a few minutes of starting, and the upper radiator hose stays cool while the engine gets hot. Cabin heat may blow cold. Common codes are P0128 and P0217.
causes2.fix: The thermostat and its gasket or housing are replaced, and the coolant is refilled and bled.

causes2.name: Cooling fan not running
causes2.tell: It runs fine on the highway but overheats sitting in traffic, in a drive-through or with the air conditioning on. The air conditioning may also cool poorly at a standstill. Codes in the P0480 to P0495 family often store.
causes2.fix: The shop tests the fan motor, relay and fuse, then replaces the fan motor or assembly, the relay or the wiring that feeds it.

causes2.name: Failed water pump
causes2.tell: Often a whine or rumble from the front of the engine, coolant dripping from behind the belt area, and overheating that gets worse quickly. On belt-driven pumps the belt area may be damp or stained.
causes2.fix: The pump and its gasket are replaced. On engines where the timing belt drives the pump, the belt and tensioner are usually done at the same time.

causes2.name: Clogged or leaking radiator
causes2.tell: Coolant drips from the front of the car, or the radiator overheats at steady speed even with a full tank and a working fan. Older cars with original coolant are the usual candidates.
causes2.fix: The radiator is replaced, the system flushed and refilled, and the hoses checked while it is apart.

causes2.name: Head gasket failure
causes2.tell: White sweet-smelling smoke from the tailpipe, bubbles in the coolant tank, coolant disappearing with no visible leak, or a rough running engine. The shop confirms it with a combustion-gas test on the coolant.
causes2.fix: The cylinder head comes off, the gasket is replaced and the head surface is checked and machined flat if needed. On a high-mileage car this is often the point where a replacement engine is compared.

engine-temperature-light.shop: First they confirm the car is cool, check the coolant level and pressure-test the cooling system to look for leaks. Then they scan for stored codes, warm the engine up on a lift or with a scan tool watching the real coolant temperature, feel the hoses to see whether the thermostat opens, and check that the fan switches on. If nothing shows up they test the coolant for combustion gases to rule out a head gasket. Expect roughly an hour, longer if a slow leak has to be left to show itself.

reset.how: This is a fault warning, not a service reminder, so there is nothing to reset. It goes out on its own once the engine cools down or the coolant is topped up, and it will come straight back the next time the engine gets hot because the cause is still there. Clearing codes with a scan tool changes nothing about the problem.
reset.note: If the light goes out after cooling, that is normal and is not a sign the fault is fixed.
