Keep your hands clear of the cooling fan and belts and do not reach down beside a warm engine. A tank that drains overnight is a leak, not a sensor problem.

diy.t: Try the washers and watch the glass
diy.how: With the car parked and in Park, switch the ignition on and pull the washer stalk for a second or two. If fluid sprays normally the pump and nozzles are fine and you are only dealing with the level. If you hear the pump buzz but nothing comes out, or you hear nothing at all, the pump or the nozzles need attention and not just a refill.

diy.t: Check for a second washer bottle
diy.how: Some wagons, SUVs and European cars have a separate rear-window washer supply, or share the front tank with headlight washers that drain it fast. Look in the owner's manual index under washer fluid to see how many fillers your car has and where they are. Filling only the front one can leave the warning on.

diy.t: Look for frozen fluid in winter
diy.how: In a hard freeze, plain water or summer fluid can turn to slush and the washers will do nothing even with the tank full. Look into the filler neck: if you see ice or slush, park the car somewhere warm until it thaws, then drain what you can by using the washers and refill with fluid rated for your coldest weather. Never pour hot water into a frozen tank.

dont: Don't fill the bottle with plain water in winter, it freezes and can split the tank, the pump or the hoses.
Don't put engine coolant, dish soap or household cleaner in the washer tank, it can swell the seals and smear the glass.
Don't keep holding the washer stalk when the tank is dry, running the pump without fluid can burn it out.
Don't set off on a salted or dusty highway with no washer fluid, the first spray from a truck can leave you unable to see.

causes2.name: Washer bottle simply run low
causes2.tell: This is by far the most common reason. Nothing else is wrong, the washers worked normally right up until the light came on, and the light goes out shortly after the tank is filled. Stores no fault code.
causes2.fix: Fill the bottle with proper washer fluid, rated for winter if you get freezing weather.

causes2.name: Failed washer fluid level sensor
causes2.tell: The light stays on, or flicks on and off over bumps, even though the bottle is full and the washers spray normally. The sensor is a small float in the side or bottom of the tank, and its connector is often buried behind the inner fender liner.
causes2.fix: The sensor is replaced, which on many cars means dropping or partly removing the washer tank to reach it.

causes2.name: Cracked or leaking washer bottle
causes2.tell: The tank empties in a day or two no matter how often you fill it, and there is a thin wet streak or a clean-washed patch on the pavement where you park. Common after a front-end knock or on older cars where the plastic has gone brittle.
causes2.fix: The washer tank is replaced, usually with the front wheel-arch liner removed to get it out.

causes2.name: Leaking pump seal or split hose
causes2.tell: Fluid drains away slowly and the washers get weak or stop spraying at all. You may see the wet area is highest near the pump at the bottom of the tank, or find a cracked hose running up to the nozzles.
causes2.fix: The pump and its rubber grommet, or the split section of hose, are replaced and the system is refilled.

causes2.name: Damaged sensor wiring or connector
causes2.tell: The warning is on with a full tank but a shop finds the sensor itself is good. Typical after work in the fender area, rodent damage, or a corroded plug sitting in road spray behind the wheel.
causes2.fix: The pin, connector or short length of wire is repaired and sealed.

washer-fluid-light.shop: A shop starts by filling the tank and seeing whether the warning clears, which settles most cases in a few minutes. If it stays on, they unplug or jumper the level sensor and check whether the dash responds, then check the sensor's wiring back to the body control module. If the tank drains instead, they fill it, wipe the area dry and leave the car parked so they can see where the fluid reappears. Expect fifteen minutes to half an hour of checking in most cases.

reset.how: There is nothing to reset. The light is driven by a float in the washer tank, so it goes out on its own once the level is back up, usually within a minute of driving or after switching the car off and on. If it is still on with a full bottle, the sensor or its wiring is faulty and clearing the message in the menu will only hide it until the next start.
reset.note: A few cars only re-read the level after a short drive, so give it a mile or two before deciding the sensor is bad.

faqs.q: Will the washer fluid light fail my state inspection?
faqs.a: The light itself is not an inspection item in any state. What can fail you is washers that do not work, since most states require the windshield washers and wipers to clean the glass. Fill the bottle and make sure both sides spray before you go.

faqs.q: Can I use water instead of washer fluid?
faqs.a: In warm weather water will get you home, but it does not cut grease or bug splatter and it grows algae in the tank. In cold weather it is a real mistake, because it freezes and can crack the tank, the pump or the lines.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the washer fluid light on?
faqs.a: As long as you like, mechanically speaking, because nothing is being damaged. The practical limit is visibility: on a salted winter road or a dusty summer highway you can lose your clear view in seconds with no fluid to spray. Treat it as a chore for this week, not an emergency.

faqs.q: The light is still on after I filled it. What now?
faqs.a: First drive a mile or switch the car off and on, because some cars only re-check the level then. If it is still lit, either the tank is leaking the fluid straight back out, which you will see as a wet patch where you park, or the float sensor in the tank has failed. Both are small jobs.

faqs.q: Is low washer fluid the same as low coolant?
faqs.a: No, and it matters. Washer fluid is for the windshield only and runs out through normal use. Coolant keeps the engine from overheating, and a low coolant warning is a real problem. If you are not sure which bottle is which, the washer cap carries a windshield-and-spray symbol.

airbag-light.look: A red or amber symbol in the main instrument cluster showing a seated person with a seat belt and a large circle in front of their chest, meant to be an inflating bag. Some makes skip the picture and light the letters SRS, AIR BAG, or a text message such as SERVICE AIR BAG instead. Do not confuse it with the separate amber PASSENGER AIR BAG OFF indicator, which is usually in the middle of the dash.
airbag-light.flash: On some older Honda, Toyota and Subaru models the light blinks in a repeating pattern instead of staying solid. The number of blinks is a code the system is trying to tell you, and a shop reads that pattern or the stored code to find the faulty part. A blinking light is no less serious than a solid one.

diy.t: Ask your dealer to check for an open airbag recall
diy.how: Your vehicle page shows recall campaigns reported for the year, make and model. Give a dealer for your brand the 17-character VIN to confirm whether an airbag recall applies and whether the repair is still open. The VIN is on the driver's door label or at the base of the windshield.

diy.t: Shake out the seat belt latches
diy.how: The buckle between the front seats has a small switch inside that tells the car whether the belt is fastened. Coins, crumbs and spilled drinks jam it. With the car parked and off, turn each buckle upside down, shake it firmly, and click the belt in and out a few times to see if it latches cleanly. Do not pour water or spray lubricant into it.

diy.t: Look for a loose yellow plug beside the front seats
diy.how: With the engine off and the key out, slide each front seat all the way forward, then all the way back, and look along the floor rails. The restraint system uses bright yellow plugs there, and they get kicked loose when something is shoved beside the seat. Only look, and tell the shop what you saw. Do not pull, push or reseat these plugs yourself, and do not run a vacuum hose over them.

diy.t: Look at the battery terminals
diy.how: With the engine off, open the hood and look at the two battery posts for loose clamps or crusty white-green buildup, since weak power can set this fault after a jump start or a flat battery. Don't pull fuses, unplug connectors or disconnect anything in the airbag system yourself. Leave that to a shop with an airbag scanner.

dont: Don't fit a steering wheel cover, phone mount or cushion over the pad in the middle of the wheel.
Don't buy a used airbag unit, steering wheel or seat from a salvage yard to fix this yourself.
Don't let anyone talk you into just clearing the code so the light goes out before a sale or an inspection.
Don't store heavy items on the front passenger seat or wedge anything under the seats while the light is on.
Don't pull airbag fuses or unplug yellow airbag connectors yourself. Done wrong, it can set off an airbag or leave it switched off.

causes2.name: Clock spring in the steering wheel
causes2.tell: The horn stops working, or works only when the wheel is at a certain angle, and the buttons on the wheel for cruise or audio go dead at the same time. It is the most common cause on cars past about ten years, because the flat ribbon of wire inside wears out from turning. A scan usually shows a driver side circuit fault.
causes2.fix: A shop removes the steering wheel, fits a new clock spring, re-centres it and clears the fault. The part is sold on its own, so the wheel and the airbag unit are reused.

causes2.name: Seat belt buckle switch
causes2.tell: The seat belt reminder chime also behaves oddly, staying on with the belt fastened or never sounding. It often starts after someone spills a drink in the console or drops change into the buckle. Common on vehicles used for ride share or with child seats in and out every day.
causes2.fix: The buckle assembly is unbolted from the seat and replaced as a unit, then the fault is cleared.

causes2.name: Wiring or connector under a front seat
causes2.tell: The light often comes on right after the seats were moved a lot, a car seat was fitted, cargo was slid under the seat, or the carpet got soaked. It can be intermittent, going out for days and coming back over a bump. Codes point at an open circuit in a side or seat circuit.
causes2.fix: A technician back probes the circuit, then repairs the broken wire or replaces the pigtail connector rather than the whole harness.

causes2.name: Passenger seat occupancy sensor or mat
causes2.tell: The PASSENGER AIR BAG OFF light stays on even with a grown adult in the seat, or flickers between on and off as they shift their weight. Known weak point on many BMW, Mercedes, Honda and Toyota models. A scan shows an occupant classification fault.
causes2.fix: The seat cushion cover comes off and the pressure mat or sensor under it is replaced, then the system is recalibrated with the maker's software.

causes2.name: Front crash sensor
causes2.tell: Usually shows up after a minor front end knock, a curb hit or a parking lot bump, including one that left no visible damage. The sensor sits behind the bumper cover or on the frame rail, where road salt and water reach it. The code names a specific front impact sensor and which side.
causes2.fix: The bumper cover or inner fender liner is loosened, the sensor is unbolted and replaced, and the torque is set to the maker's figure because a loose sensor reads the crash wrong.

causes2.name: Airbag control module
causes2.tell: Several unrelated faults appear at once, or the module reports an internal fault that will not clear. On a car that was in a crash where anything deployed, the module locks itself with a crash record stored and the light will not go out even after all the hardware is replaced.
causes2.fix: The module is replaced and programmed to the car, or on many vehicles the original is sent out to be reset and reinstalled.

airbag-light.shop: The first step is a scan with a tool that can read the restraint system, which a basic code reader cannot do. The stored code names the circuit, then the technician checks power and ground at the suspect connector and wiggles the harness to find a break, and runs the VIN for open recalls at the same time. Expect roughly an hour for a straightforward fault, and longer for an intermittent one that only appears over bumps, because the car may need to be driven or the harness shaken while the tool watches live data.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a reminder, so there is nothing here that is meant to be reset. A scan tool can switch the light off for a moment, but the system tests itself every time you start the car, so the light comes straight back until the broken part is fixed. The one exception works the other way: after a crash the control module may hold a permanent record that keeps the light on even once everything is repaired, and that module has to be replaced or professionally reset.
reset.note: Don't use airbag-light bypass resistors or code-clearing tricks. They only hide the fault and can leave you with no airbag protection in a crash.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive with the airbag light on?
faqs.a: The car itself drives normally, so you are not stranded. What you have lost is the crash protection: with this light on, assume the airbags and the belt tensioners may not fire at all, or may fire when they should not. Wear your seat belt and have it checked right away, as owner's manuals advise.

faqs.q: Will my airbags still work with the light on?
faqs.a: Treat them as not working. The system turned the light on because it tested itself and found something wrong, and it cannot tell you how much still works. Sometimes only one part is offline, but the only way to know is to have the stored codes read.

faqs.q: Will it pass inspection?
faqs.a: It depends entirely on where you live. In most states the emissions test ignores this light completely, but states that do a full safety inspection can and do fail a car for it. Check your own state's rules before you book the test.

faqs.q: Does this mean my car has a recall?
faqs.a: The warning light alone cannot establish recall coverage. Your vehicle page lists campaigns for the model year. A dealer can check your VIN and confirm coverage before you approve a paid repair.

faqs.q: Can a mechanic just turn the light off?
faqs.a: They can clear the code, but it is not a repair and an honest shop will tell you so. The system retests itself at every start, so the light returns within a few seconds to a few drives. If a shop offers to kill the light for a flat fee without naming the faulty part, go somewhere else.

check-engine-light.look: It sits in the main instrument cluster, usually near the middle, and is shaped like the side view of an engine block with small bumps along the top. It is almost always amber or yellow. Some makes skip the symbol and print the words SERVICE ENGINE SOON, CHECK ENGINE or ENGINE in the display, and a few show a plain outline of an engine with a lightning bolt or an exclamation mark inside it.
check-engine-light.flash: A flashing or blinking check engine light is more serious than a steady one. It means the engine is misfiring badly and unburned fuel is passing into the exhaust, which can overheat and ruin the catalytic converter in a matter of minutes. Ease off the gas, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't keep driving; have it towed or checked before you go further.

diy.t: Tighten the gas cap
diy.how: With the engine off, unscrew the fuel cap and screw it back on until it clicks at least once. Look at the rubber seal around the edge: if it is cracked, hard or missing, the cap is not sealing and needs replacing. A loose or worn cap is one of the most common reasons this light comes on, and the light may take a few days of normal driving to go out on its own.

diy.t: Get the trouble code read
diy.how: The engine computer stored a code that says which system it is unhappy about. Write the code down exactly, letter and all four digits, then look it up on our code lookup before you agree to any repair.
diy.tools: None, or a basic code reader

diy.t: Notice how the car is behaving
diy.how: Before you call anyone, make a short list of what the car is doing. Is the idle rough or shaky, is there a smell of fuel or rotten eggs, does it hesitate when you press the gas, is it using more fuel than usual, does it only happen when cold or when the air conditioning is on? A shop can get to the real fault far faster with that list, which keeps your diagnosis time down.

diy.t: Look for something obviously loose in the engine bay
diy.how: With the engine off and cool, open the hood and look across the top of the engine for a rubber air hose that has popped off, a plastic connector hanging loose, or an air filter box lid that is not clipped down. Push anything like that back on by hand until it seats. Do not pull wires apart to inspect them, and leave anything hot, pressurised or hidden from view for a shop.

dont: Don't keep driving while the light is flashing; you can overheat and melt the catalytic converter, which can start a fire.
Don't disconnect the battery to make the light go away. The fault comes straight back and you wipe out the stored code a shop needs to find it.
Don't let a steady light sit for months. A small sensor fault or misfire left alone is what kills catalytic converters.
Don't book an emissions test with the light on. In most states a lit check engine light is an automatic fail, test fee included.

causes2.name: Loose, cracked or worn gas cap (small EVAP leak)
causes2.tell: No change in how the car drives, and often it appears a day or two after filling up. The stored code is usually one of the evaporative emissions leak codes such as P0455 or P0442. The cap may feel loose or its rubber seal may look dry and cracked.
causes2.fix: Tighten the cap, or fit a new one if the seal is damaged. If a new cap does not fix it, a shop smoke-tests the fuel tank and vent lines for a leaking hose or valve.

causes2.name: Failed oxygen sensor
causes2.tell: Fuel economy slips, the idle may be slightly uneven, and the exhaust can smell richer than normal. Codes usually point at a sensor circuit or a fuel mixture that is too rich or too lean, such as P0171. The car often still drives fine, which is why people put this one off.
causes2.fix: The faulty sensor is unscrewed from the exhaust and a new one fitted.

causes2.name: Misfire from worn spark plugs or a failed ignition coil
causes2.tell: The engine shakes at idle, stumbles when you accelerate, and may lose noticeable power. This is the usual cause when the light is flashing. Codes are in the misfire family, P0300 for a random misfire or P0301 through P0308 for a named cylinder.
causes2.fix: The failed coil is replaced and the spark plugs are usually renewed as a set at the same time, since worn plugs are what kill coils.

causes2.name: Mass airflow sensor fault
causes2.tell: Hesitation when pulling away, surging idle, sometimes a stall just after start-up, and worse fuel economy. The code names the mass airflow circuit or an air and fuel mixture that is out of range. A dirty air filter or a split intake hose often sits behind it.
causes2.fix: The sensor is cleaned or replaced and the air filter and intake hoses are checked, since a split hose will cause the same symptom again.

causes2.name: EVAP purge or vent valve stuck
causes2.tell: Usually no symptoms at all, though some cars idle oddly or are hard to restart straight after refuelling. The code points at the purge or vent valve circuit or at a leak the smoke test traces to the valve rather than the cap.
causes2.fix: The stuck valve is replaced. It is a small part bolted to the engine bay or near the fuel tank, and the work is typically under an hour.

causes2.name: Failed catalytic converter
causes2.tell: Often no driving symptoms early on, then sluggish acceleration and a sulphur or rotten egg smell. The classic code is P0420 or P0430. A converter rarely dies on its own, so a shop should also find what killed it, usually a long-running misfire or oil burning.
causes2.fix: The converter section of the exhaust is replaced, and the underlying cause is repaired first so the new one is not destroyed too.

check-engine-light.shop: A shop plugs a scan tool into the socket beneath the dash, pulls every stored code plus the freeze frame data that shows what the engine was doing the moment the fault was recorded, then clears nothing and goes looking. From there it is live data, a smoke test for an evaporative leak, or a cylinder and ignition test for a misfire. Expect roughly half an hour for a simple one and up to two hours for an intermittent fault that has to be reproduced on a test drive.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a service reminder, so there is nothing you are meant to reset. A code reader or a battery disconnect will switch the light off for a while, but it has repaired nothing: the engine computer runs the same self-test again over the next few drives and the light comes back as soon as it sees the fault. Clearing it also wipes the stored code and the freeze frame data, which makes the fault harder to find. The one exception is a genuine fix such as tightening a loose gas cap, after which the light often goes out by itself within a few days of normal driving.
reset.note: Clearing codes also resets the emissions readiness monitors, and most states will not pass the car until those have reset themselves over several days of mixed driving.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the check engine light on?
faqs.a: If it is flashing, or the car is shaking, losing power or smells of fuel, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. If the light is steady and the car drives, idles and sounds normal, you can usually finish your trip and book a scan within the next week or so.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the check engine light on?
faqs.a: In most states, no. An emissions or safety inspection that reads the engine computer fails the car automatically when the light is lit, whatever the reason. Fix the fault first, then drive the car for several days so the computer finishes its self-tests before you book the test.

faqs.q: Does the check engine light reset itself?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If the fault was something that truly went away, such as a gas cap you tightened, the computer needs to pass the same self-test a few times before it turns the light off, which usually takes two or three days of ordinary driving. If the fault is still there, the light stays on.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive at night with the check engine light on?
faqs.a: The light itself has nothing to do with your lights, brakes or steering. The real question is how the car is running: if the light is flashing, the engine is misfiring or it's losing power, pull over and turn the engine off, because being stranded on a dark road is the danger. Get it sorted before a long night trip.

faqs.q: Why is my check engine light on with no symptoms?
faqs.a: That is very common and usually good news. Evaporative emissions faults, a slightly lazy oxygen sensor and a stuck purge valve all trigger the light while the car drives perfectly. It still needs reading, because the computer uses the same light for small faults and serious ones.

coolant-level-light.look: An amber symbol low in the cluster: a squared-off tank or radiator shape with wavy lines across the bottom, and on many European cars a small thermometer poking out of it. VW, Audi and Volvo often print 'Check coolant level' in the driver display instead of showing a symbol. Plenty of cars have no separate coolant light at all, and a low level shows up as the red temperature warning or a general warning triangle.

diy.t: Read the overflow tank level with the engine cold
diy.how: Wait until the engine is cold to the touch, then find the see-through plastic tank in the engine bay with MIN and MAX lines moulded into the side. You read it through the plastic, so nothing needs opening. If the coolant sits below the MIN line, or you cannot see any liquid at all, you have your answer. Check it in the morning before the car has run, because the level rises as the engine warms up.

diy.t: Top up the overflow tank, cold engine only
diy.how: With the engine stone cold, open only the cap on the plastic overflow tank, never the radiator cap, and pour in pre-mixed coolant of the type named in your owner's manual until it reaches the MAX line. Color is not a safe guide, so match the specification rather than the shade. Buying it pre-mixed means there is nothing to measure. Refit the cap firmly, run the engine, let it cool right down and check the level once more.
diy.tools: A bottle of the correct pre-mixed coolant

diy.t: Check the ground where you park for drips
diy.how: Look at the spot the car sits overnight. Coolant dries into a crusty stain, is usually bright green, orange or pink, and smells faintly sweet. A patch near the front middle points at the radiator or a hose, while a stain further back on one side is often a heater hose. Finding a stain turns a vague warning into something a shop can go straight to.

diy.t: Watch the temperature gauge on your next drive
diy.how: Before you set off, note where the needle normally sits, then keep half an eye on it. If it climbs past the middle, or a red temperature warning appears, pull over and switch the engine off straight away, because that is a far more urgent problem than a low level warning. A needle that stays where it always sits means you have a little time to get the leak found.

dont: Don't open the radiator cap, or any cap, on a warm engine. The coolant is under pressure and sprays out hot enough to scald badly.
Don't keep topping up with plain tap water. It waters down the antifreeze and rusts the cooling system from the inside.
Don't assume it is fine because the temperature gauge looks normal. The gauge needs coolant touching it to read correctly.
Don't pour in stop-leak powder to hide the leak before anyone has found where the coolant is actually going.

causes2.name: Leaking hose, clamp or hose connection
causes2.tell: The most common reason, especially on cars past about eight years old. Look for a crusty coloured stain or a damp patch at the end of a rubber hose, and a hose that feels spongy or rock hard rather than firm. The level drops slowly over weeks rather than overnight.
causes2.fix: Replace the failed hose or tighten and renew the clamp, then refill the system and bleed the air out so there are no pockets left behind.

causes2.name: Leaking radiator or radiator end tank
causes2.tell: A stain or wet trail at the front of the engine bay, often where the plastic top tank meets the metal core, and a sweet smell after a drive. Many cars drip only when hot and pressurised, so the leak can hide while the engine is cold.
causes2.fix: Replace the radiator. Repairing a cracked plastic end tank rarely lasts. The job includes new coolant and bleeding the system, and sometimes a hose that has gone hard with age.

causes2.name: Leaking water pump
causes2.tell: Coolant residue or a drip coming from the pump area at the front or side of the engine, often with a faint whine or rumble from a worn bearing. On engines where the pump is driven by the timing belt, the first sign can be coolant appearing low with no visible drip outside.
causes2.fix: Replace the water pump, and on timing belt engines replace the belt and tensioner at the same time because they come apart together. Then refill and bleed the system.

causes2.name: Faulty coolant level sensor
causes2.tell: The giveaway is a warning that does not match reality: the tank is right up at the MAX line, the engine never gets hot, but the light stays on or flickers on and off over bumps. Sometimes it is only the float or the connector rather than the sensor itself.
causes2.fix: Replace the sensor, which usually screws or clips into the bottom or side of the overflow tank, after checking the wiring and connector for corrosion.

causes2.name: Cracked overflow tank or a bad pressure cap
causes2.tell: A hairline crack in the plastic tank that only weeps under pressure, or a cap whose rubber seal has gone hard. A weak cap lets coolant boil over and escape as steam, so the level falls with nothing ever dripping on the ground.
causes2.fix: Fit a new tank or a new cap with the correct pressure rating stamped on it.

causes2.name: Head gasket or internal coolant leak
causes2.tell: The level keeps falling with nothing on the ground. Other signs are white sweet-smelling smoke from the exhaust once warm, bubbles in the overflow tank while it idles, a milky look to the engine oil, or the car running rough on a cold start.
causes2.fix: The cylinder head comes off, the gasket is replaced and the head is checked for flatness and cracks.

coolant-level-light.shop: A shop confirms the level and the condition of the coolant, then pressure tests the system: a hand pump goes on the filler neck, they raise it to the pressure printed on the cap and watch whether it holds. A drop means a leak, and they trace it with a bright light, with dye, or by looking for crusty residue at the hoses, the water pump and the radiator. They test the cap too, since a weak one lets coolant escape as steam. If nothing leaks outside, they check for exhaust gases in the coolant to rule the head gasket in or out. A pressure test and visual check takes under an hour.

reset.how: This is a fault warning, not a service reminder, so there is nothing you are meant to reset. Once the coolant is back at the full mark and the engine has run and cooled again, the light goes out by itself, usually within a drive or two. If you top it up and the light comes straight back, either the coolant is escaping somewhere or the level sensor is bad, and no reset procedure fixes either one.
reset.note: Some cars only check the level on a cold start with the car parked, so give it one cold start before deciding the light is stuck on.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the low coolant light on?
faqs.a: Not far until you've checked it. Once the engine is cool, read the tank level. If it's only a little low, top it up and get the leak checked within days. If the tank is empty, the light is red or says stop, or the temperature gauge climbs, don't drive it.

faqs.q: Can I just add water instead of coolant?
faqs.a: In an emergency, water will get you to a shop, and distilled water is better than tap water. But coolant also stops the system freezing, raises the boiling point and protects the metal inside from corrosion, so plain water is a get-home measure only. Have it drained and filled properly with the right mix soon after.

faqs.q: Will the light go off by itself once I top it up?
faqs.a: Usually yes, within a drive or two, once the level is back above the sensor and the engine has been through a warm-up and cool-down. If it stays on with a full tank, suspect the sensor or its wiring. If it goes out and returns in a few weeks, the coolant is leaking and the leak needs finding.

faqs.q: Why is my coolant low when I cannot see any leak?
faqs.a: Three common reasons. A leak that only opens up when the system is hot and pressurised, so it evaporates off a hot engine and never reaches the ground. A weak pressure cap letting coolant out as steam. Or an internal leak at the head gasket, where the coolant is being burned in the engine. A pressure test tells them apart.

faqs.q: Is the low coolant light the same as the red temperature light?
faqs.a: Not always. On many cars an amber coolant light means the level is low and the red temperature light means the engine is already too hot. But some cars, including many Volkswagens and Audis, show a red coolant light for low coolant and say to stop. If any coolant or temperature light is red, pull over and switch off, then check your owner's manual.

cruise-control-light.look: A green or white symbol in the cluster, most often a speedometer dial with an arrow or a needle, and on some makes just the word CRUISE. Many cars show one color when the system is awake and a second color, or the set speed as a number, once a speed is locked in. Amber, or the symbol with a line through it, means the system is not available.
cruise-control-light.flash: A cruise symbol that flashes, or turns amber, is the car saying the system has dropped out or cannot be used right now. Adaptive cruise does this when the radar behind the grille is covered in snow, spray or mud. Plain cruise does it when the car sees a fault in the brake switch or in the road speed signal. Either way it is a report, not normal operation.

diy.t: Check your brake lights
diy.how: Have someone stand behind the parked car while you press the brake pedal, or back up close to a garage door at night and watch the red glow in the mirror. Both brake lights should come on and go off with the pedal. The same small switch at the top of the brake pedal that lights those lamps also tells cruise to let go, and a bad one stops cruise setting at all.
diy.tools: A helper, or a wall to reflect off

diy.t: Wipe the radar area in the grille
diy.how: On a car with adaptive cruise, walk to the front while it is parked and find the smooth plastic panel or the badge in the middle of the grille or the lower bumper. Wipe mud, slush, road salt and bugs off it with a damp cloth. Do not pry the cover off, and do not fit a plate frame or an accessory in front of it.

diy.t: Check the fuse for the cruise or stop lamp circuit
diy.how: Open the cabin fuse box, usually behind a cover at the end of the dash or below the glovebox, and read the map printed on the lid. With the car switched off, pull the fuse marked cruise, stop lamp or brake switch and look at the metal strip inside. A broken strip means it has blown. Replace it only with the same number.
diy.tools: Owner's manual and a fuse puller

diy.t: Try the buttons and read the rules for your car
diy.how: Cruise will not set below a certain speed, in a low gear, with a door open, or while traction control is working. Press the on button and watch for the symbol, then try to set a speed on a clear, dry road at normal highway pace. Look in the owner's manual index under cruise control for the limits your particular car has.

dont: Don't use cruise control on wet, icy or snow covered roads; it can hold power on right through a skid.
Don't treat adaptive cruise as self driving; keep your hands on the wheel and your eyes on the road.
Don't tap the brakes just to test whether cruise cancels while a car is close behind you.
Don't ignore a cruise fault when your brake lights are out too, because one switch feeds both.

causes2.name: Cruise control is simply engaged
causes2.tell: The symbol appeared right after you pressed the cruise button, and the car is holding a steady speed on its own without your foot on the pedal. Nothing is wrong; it is doing its job.
causes2.fix: Nothing. Press cancel or tap the brake and the symbol goes out.

causes2.name: Failed brake light switch
causes2.tell: Cruise refuses to set, or drops out the moment you set it. Often the brake lights stay off, or stay on all the time, and the stored code names the brake switch circuit. On many cars the shifter also refuses to come out of park.
causes2.fix: A small switch clipped to the bracket at the top of the brake pedal is unplugged and replaced, then adjusted.

causes2.name: Snow, slush or mud over the front radar
causes2.tell: Adaptive cruise goes unavailable during a storm or after a salty winter drive, and the dash shows a message about a blocked front sensor. It comes back by itself once the grille area is clean and dry.
causes2.fix: Wiping the radar cover clean. No parts needed.

causes2.name: Front radar sensor failed or knocked out of aim
causes2.tell: Adaptive cruise stays unavailable on a clean, dry day, usually after a front end bump or a curb strike, and the scan tool shows the radar module not answering or reporting itself out of alignment.
causes2.fix: The radar unit behind the grille is re-aimed or replaced, then calibrated to the car.

causes2.name: Faulty cruise switch or steering wheel wiring
causes2.tell: Nothing happens at all when you press the buttons on the wheel, or they work only now and then. If the horn or the wheel audio buttons act up at the same time, the coiled wiring behind the wheel is the suspect rather than the switch.
causes2.fix: The switch pad on the steering wheel, or the coiled connector behind it, is replaced.

causes2.name: Wheel speed sensor or throttle fault
causes2.tell: Cruise will not set and the speedometer flickers, or the ABS and traction lights are on alongside it. Cruise needs a road speed signal it can trust, so it shuts itself off when the car cannot agree on how fast it is going.
causes2.fix: The faulty wheel speed sensor, or the throttle or pedal sensor behind it, is replaced.

cruise-control-light.shop: A shop reads the codes first, then checks the shared parts that fail most: brake lights on and off with the pedal, the brake switch adjustment at the top of the pedal, and whether road speed stays steady on live data. On a car with adaptive cruise they also check the radar behind the grille for codes, damage and alignment, and see whether the windshield camera is tied in. Half an hour to an hour is typical, longer when they have to road test to catch an intermittent fault.

reset.how: Cruise control has no reset procedure. The green symbol simply follows the system, so it lights when cruise is on and goes out when you cancel it or switch the car off. If the symbol is amber or the car says cruise is unavailable, that is a fault report, and clearing codes or disconnecting the battery will not repair it; the car checks itself again and the message returns. A blocked radar is the one exception, and that clears itself once the sensor is clean.
reset.note: Some makes remember that cruise was on when you last parked, while others start every drive with the system switched off.

faqs.q: Why won't my cruise control set?
faqs.a: Start with the brake lights. The switch on the brake pedal cancels cruise, and when it fails the car believes your foot is on the brake all the time. Cars also refuse to set below a certain speed, in a low gear, or while traction control is working. If the brake lights are fine and the road is clear, it needs a scan.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive with the cruise light on?
faqs.a: A green or white cruise symbol is information, not a warning, and it says nothing about the engine, the brakes or the steering. If it is amber or flashing, the car is telling you cruise is unavailable; carry on driving and have it looked at when it suits you.

faqs.q: Will a cruise control fault fail inspection?
faqs.a: The cruise system itself is not part of a state safety or emissions inspection. The brake light switch behind many cruise faults is another matter, because brake lights that do not work will fail an inspection and are a ticket on their own. Fix the switch and both problems go away together.

faqs.q: Does adaptive cruise control drive the car for me?
faqs.a: No. It holds a set gap to the car in front and slows down and speeds up to keep it, but you steer, you watch the road, and you are responsible. It can miss a stopped vehicle, a motorcycle between lanes or a sharp cut in, so keep your hands on the wheel.

faqs.q: Can I use cruise control in the rain?
faqs.a: Better not. Holding a steady speed on a wet or icy road can keep power going to the wheels through a skid, which is exactly when you want a human foot on the pedal instead. Save cruise for dry roads with light traffic.

electronic-parking-brake-light.look: It shows in the main cluster near the other brake lights: an amber circle with a P inside, usually with small brackets on each side and often an exclamation mark. Several makes show no symbol at all and instead light the general amber warning lamp with a written message such as park brake malfunction or service parking brake. The matching red P light is the normal one that means the brake is applied.
electronic-parking-brake-light.flash: On some cars the parking brake light blinks rather than staying on. A blinking light means the brake has not finished applying or releasing, so the car is not being held properly. Set it and release it once more, and if it keeps blinking, do not leave the car on a slope relying on it.

diy.t: Cycle the parking brake switch
diy.how: Park on flat ground, leave the car running and in Park, and keep your foot firmly on the brake pedal. Press the parking brake switch down to release, then pull it up to set, then release it again. Do that twice. Many cars clear a one-off glitch this way. If the light is still on after two tries, stop: pressing it over and over will not help.

diy.t: Unplug the charging cable
diy.how: On electric and plug-in hybrid cars the parking brake is held on deliberately while the charging cable is connected, and a cable that is still plugged in or not seated properly can look like a fault. Unplug it at the car, close the charge flap, then start the car and look at the light again.

diy.t: Check the 12-volt battery
diy.how: A weak 12-volt battery sets this light off on a lot of cars, especially after the car has sat for a while or been jump started. With the engine off, look at the two battery terminals: they should be clean and tight enough that you cannot twist the clamp by hand. If the engine cranks slowly or the lights dim, get the battery and charging system tested at a parts store.

diy.t: Feel for a dragging rear wheel
diy.how: Drive slowly a few minutes, park, and hold the back of your hand a few inches away from each rear wheel without touching the brake parts. If one side gives off much more heat than the other, or there is a hot metal smell, the parking brake is still clamped on that corner. Don't keep driving it: that cause ruins pads and rotors quickly.

diy.t: Look up your car's own message
diy.how: Open the owner's manual, or the PDF version on your phone, and find the warning light pages. Makes word this differently and some tell you a specific recovery step, such as how to release the brake manually or that the car must go on a flatbed. It also tells you whether your car has auto hold, which uses the same system and the same light.

dont: Don't park on a hill trusting this brake: use Park or first gear and turn the front wheels into the curb.
Don't jab the switch repeatedly if the brake won't release: you can overheat the little motors at the rear wheels.
Don't try to drag the car along with the brake stuck on: have it flatbedded instead.
Don't let a shop fit rear brake pads without a scan tool, as the brake motors must be wound back and reset electronically.

causes2.name: Failed parking brake actuator motor at a rear wheel
causes2.tell: You hear the whirring noise from only one side, or from neither, when the brake sets. The car usually stores a code naming the left or right actuator circuit, and that same wheel may stay clamped or never clamp at all.
causes2.fix: Replace the actuator motor, or the whole rear caliper on cars where the motor is built in, then recalibrate the system with a scan tool.

causes2.name: Weak or failing 12-volt battery
causes2.tell: The light shows up with a handful of other warnings at once, often after the car sat for a week or was jump started, and the engine cranks slowly. A battery test at a parts store shows it down on cranking power.
causes2.fix: Replace the battery, and on many European cars register the new one to the car so the charging system treats it correctly.

causes2.name: Broken parking brake switch
causes2.tell: The switch feels dead or loose, nothing happens when you press it, and the code points to the switch circuit rather than a wheel. Common on cars where the switch sits next to the gear lever and gets knocked.
causes2.fix: Replace the switch assembly in the console, then check that the brake sets and releases normally.

causes2.name: Worn rear brake pads or a sticking caliper
causes2.tell: The brake motors run longer than normal or stall out because there is nothing left to clamp, and you hear grinding when braking. One rear wheel may run hot and the car pulls slightly.
causes2.fix: Replace the rear pads, and rotors if needed, with the parking brake motors retracted by a scan tool, then reset the system.

causes2.name: Damaged wiring or corroded connector at a rear wheel
causes2.tell: The light comes and goes, often over bumps or after rain, and the code jumps between an open and a short on one actuator. The flexible loom that runs to the rear caliper is a known rub and corrosion point.
causes2.fix: Repair or replace the damaged section of wiring and the connector, then clear the code and test the brake.

causes2.name: Parking brake or ABS control module fault
causes2.tell: It shows up with the ABS and traction control lights together, and the scan tool cannot talk to the brake module or reports an internal failure inside it.
causes2.fix: Replace the control module and program it to the car, which needs dealer-level software on most makes.

electronic-parking-brake-light.shop: A shop plugs in a scan tool that can talk to the parking brake module, reads the stored codes, and watches the live data while they command the brake on and off. That tells them straight away whether a wheel actuator is answering, whether the switch is sending a signal, and whether system voltage dropped. They check battery condition and rear pad thickness at the same time. Reckon on half an hour to an hour of diagnosis.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a service reminder, so there is nothing for you to reset. Clearing the code with a scan tool or pulling the battery cable may make the light go out for a trip, but it comes back as soon as the car tests the brake again, and in the meantime the brake still may not hold. After a real repair the shop has to run the parking brake relearn or calibration with a scan tool, which winds the motors back out to the right position.
reset.note: Cars with auto hold use the same system, so that feature usually stops working until the fault is fixed.

faqs.q: How do I release an electronic parking brake that is stuck on?
faqs.a: Try the normal release once more with the engine running, your foot on the brake pedal and the car in Park, then check that no charging cable is plugged in and that the 12-volt battery is not flat. If it still will not let go, stop there. Most makes say the car has to go on a flatbed, because the release is done through the brake module with a scan tool.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with an EPB fault light on?
faqs.a: In states that inspect brakes or look at dashboard warning lights, an amber parking brake fault is likely to fail, and a parking brake that does not hold the car fails on its own in states that test it. Expect to fix the cause first.

faqs.q: Does the light go off by itself if I disconnect the battery?
faqs.a: It might go out for a short while, but it is not fixed. The car retests the parking brake every time you use it and relights the warning when it finds the same problem. Disconnecting the battery can also wipe radio presets and make a weak battery situation worse.

faqs.q: Why did this light come on right after I changed my rear brakes?
faqs.a: The parking brake motors have to be wound back electronically before the rear pads come out, and wound back in and calibrated afterwards. If that was skipped, or done by hand, the system reads the wrong position and sets the fault. A shop with the right scan tool can usually run the calibration and clear it.

epc-light.look: Not a picture but three amber letters, EPC, usually low in the middle of the cluster or just under the rev counter. Older Volkswagens and Audis print the letters plain; newer ones show a small amber engine outline with EPC underneath, and a few spell out a message like Electronic Power Control Fault on the driver display instead.

diy.t: Shut the engine off and restart it
diy.how: Park somewhere safe, switch the engine fully off and wait about half a minute so the computers go to sleep. Start it again and see whether EPC stays lit. If it clears and the car pulls normally, the fault was a passing one, but the code is still saved and worth reading.

diy.t: Check whether your brake lights work
diy.how: A failing brake pedal switch is the single most common cause of EPC on these cars. With the car parked, the parking brake set and the engine off, turn the key to the on position, then have someone stand behind the car while you press the brake pedal. If the brake lights do not come on, stay on, or the cruise control has stopped working, tell the shop: that points straight at the switch.

diy.t: Check the battery terminals and battery age
diy.how: With the engine off and cool, look at the two battery posts. White or green crust, or a cable clamp you can move by hand, means poor power to the computers, and a tired battery on a Volkswagen or Audi can set odd faults across several systems. Snug the clamp nuts gently with a small wrench, and if the battery is more than about five years old mention that too.

diy.t: Look for a loose air hose on a cold engine
diy.how: With the engine off and cold, open the hood and look at the wide plastic or rubber pipe that runs from the air filter box to the engine. Check that both ends are pushed on and the clamps are tight, and look for a split in the folds of the pipe. A pipe that has popped off lets in unmeasured air, which upsets the throttle system and can set EPC.
diy.tools: None, or a screwdriver for a clamp

dont: Don't drive at highway speed in reduced power; the car may not accelerate when you need it to.
Don't disconnect the battery to clear EPC, because the fault returns and you may lose radio and window settings.
Don't assume the brake switch is fine just because your brake lights work; it can fail in a way only a scan tool sees.
Don't keep driving for weeks with EPC and a misfire, as raw fuel can wreck the catalytic converter.

causes2.name: Failed brake pedal (brake light) switch
causes2.tell: Classic signs are cruise control that will not set, brake lights that stay on or stay off, or a car that will not come out of park. EPC often appears with the ABS or stability light. A scan tool shows the switch sending two readings that do not agree.
causes2.fix: A small plug-in switch at the top of the brake pedal is pulled out and a new one clicked in, then the fault is cleared.

causes2.name: Dirty or failed throttle body
causes2.tell: The idle hunts up and down, the pedal feels slow or dead, and power is capped. Codes about throttle position or throttle adaptation are stored. A shop can often see the throttle plate refusing to follow the pedal on live data.
causes2.fix: Sometimes the throttle body is cleaned and re-taught to the computer. If the motor inside it is worn out, the whole unit is replaced and adapted.

causes2.name: Misfire from worn coils or spark plugs
causes2.tell: The engine shakes at idle, stumbles under load, and the check engine light usually joins EPC. Coil packs on these engines are a known weak point. Codes name the cylinder that is missing, such as P0302.
causes2.fix: The failed ignition coils and the spark plugs are replaced, normally as a set so the rest do not fail next month.

causes2.name: Mass airflow sensor fault
causes2.tell: Power falls off at higher speeds, fuel use climbs, and the engine may stall when you lift off. The car often runs better for a moment after the battery is disconnected. Codes point at air mass or fuel mixture being out of range.
causes2.fix: The sensor in the intake pipe after the air filter is unclipped and replaced. A split intake pipe is checked at the same time.

causes2.name: Accelerator pedal position sensor
causes2.tell: Acceleration lags or drops out with no warning, and sometimes the engine will not rev at all in park. The stored code names pedal position, and live data shows the pedal signal jumping about when the pedal is moved slowly.
causes2.fix: The pedal assembly with its sensor built in is unbolted from the footwell and replaced, then the computer relearns its rest position.

causes2.name: ABS wheel speed or brake pressure sensor
causes2.tell: EPC shows up alongside the ABS and stability lights, the speedometer may drop out, and the stability system clicks or cuts power in corners. Codes come from the brake control unit rather than the engine, which is why a basic engine-only scanner finds nothing.
causes2.fix: The faulty wheel speed sensor or brake pressure sensor is replaced.

epc-light.shop: The first move is a full scan with a tool that can talk to all the Volkswagen Group computers, not just the engine, because EPC is often set by the brake, stability or steering module and a basic code reader will show nothing at all. From there the shop checks the brake pedal switch, battery voltage, and live throttle and pedal readings, and looks up any factory software updates for that model. That first look usually takes about an hour, and longer if the fault only appears while driving.

reset.how: EPC is a fault light, not a service reminder, so there is nothing to reset. Clearing the code with a scan tool, or leaving the battery disconnected, puts the light out for a while but repairs nothing, and it comes straight back once the computer sees the same problem again. It also wipes the stored data a technician would use to find the fault. Fix the cause and the light goes out by itself, often within a drive or two.
reset.note: Some of these faults need the throttle or pedal re-taught to the computer with a scan tool after the part is replaced.

faqs.q: Will the EPC light clear on its own?
faqs.a: It sometimes does, if the fault was momentary and the computer stops seeing it after a few starts. The code stays in memory, so a shop can still read what happened. A light that keeps coming back is a real fault that will not go away without a repair.

faqs.q: Is EPC the same as the check engine light?
faqs.a: No, though they often come on together. The check engine light covers the engine and emissions, while EPC covers the electronic throttle system, which includes the gas pedal, cruise control, and on many models the brake and stability inputs too. EPC can be on with the check engine light off, and the other way round.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the EPC light on?
faqs.a: It depends on your state's rules, so check your local ones. EPC itself is not the emissions light, but it very often comes with a check engine light, and that will fail an emissions test. A car stuck in reduced power can also fail a safety check because it cannot be driven properly.

faqs.q: Why is my VW suddenly so slow with EPC on?
faqs.a: Once the computer stops trusting a throttle, pedal or brake reading, it deliberately holds power back to protect the engine. That is the car being cautious rather than the engine failing. Normal power almost always returns as soon as the faulty sensor or switch is replaced.

esp-bas-light.look: Amber block letters reading ESP BAS, usually in the message area next to or under the speedometer rather than a drawn symbol. Some years write it ESP/BAS or stack it on two lines, and a few show a text message such as ESP/BAS DEACTIVATED. On most Chrysler, Dodge, Jeep and Ram models the skidding-car traction light, and often the ABS light, come on at the same time.
esp-bas-light.flash: The ESP BAS letters stay on steady. The skidding-car light beside them flashing while you drive is a different thing: that is stability control actually catching a slide, which is the system working, not a fault.

diy.t: Check your brake lights
diy.how: Park, leave the engine off with the key on, and have someone stand behind the car while you press the brake pedal. If the brake lights do not come on, or only one does, the switch above the brake pedal is a prime suspect and is usually a quick shop fix. You may also notice cruise control no longer works or the car fights being shifted out of park.

diy.t: Look at the brake fluid level
diy.how: With the engine off and cool, find the small see-through brake fluid tank, usually at the back of the engine bay on the driver's side. The fluid should sit between the MIN and MAX marks on the side. If it is at or below MIN, the brakes need looking at before anything else. Do not open the cap: you only need to read the level through the plastic.

diy.t: Restart the car and check the battery posts
diy.how: Shut the car off, wait a minute and start it again. A one-off drop in voltage, like a slow crank on a cold morning, can set this light and it may not come back. While the engine is off, look at the two battery terminals: they should be clean and tight, with no white or green fluff and no wobble when you nudge the cable by hand.

diy.t: Try the steering wheel relearn
diy.how: If the light appeared right after a battery change, a jump start or an alignment, the steering angle sensor may just need to find center again. With the car parked and the engine idling, turn the steering wheel all the way to the left, then all the way to the right, then back to straight ahead. Switch the engine off, restart it, and drive straight for a few minutes. If the light goes out and stays out, that was it.

dont: Don't drive hard, tow, or push on in rain or snow while it's on; nothing will catch the car if a wheel slips.
Don't leave it for weeks. The same fault usually shuts off ABS too, so the wheels can lock up in a hard stop.
Don't just clear the code and call it fixed; it comes back as soon as the system sees the fault again.
Don't keep driving if the red brake warning light joins it or the pedal feels different.

causes2.name: Failing brake light switch
causes2.tell: The brake lights don't work, or cruise control quits, or the car resists shifting out of park. Codes point at the brake switch circuit. This is the classic cause on Jeep Grand Cherokee, Dodge Charger and Chrysler 300.
causes2.fix: A new switch clips in above the brake pedal, then the stored codes are cleared. It is a quick job on most of these cars.

causes2.name: Wheel speed sensor or its wiring
causes2.tell: The ABS and skidding-car lights are on as well, the speedometer may drop out for a second as you roll to a stop, and the code names one particular wheel. Often rust or a wire chafed through near the wheel.
causes2.fix: The wheel comes off and the sensor at that corner is replaced, or the broken bit of wiring is repaired.

causes2.name: Steering angle sensor out of calibration or failed
causes2.tell: It showed up right after a battery change, a jump start, an alignment or steering column work, and the code mentions the steering angle. Sometimes a full lock-to-lock turn and restart clears it.
causes2.fix: A shop recalibrates the sensor with a scan tool. If the sensor itself has failed it is replaced behind the steering wheel and then calibrated.

causes2.name: Weak battery or poor battery connection
causes2.tell: Several warning lights came on together, often during a slow crank or after the car sat for days, and they clear for a while after a drive. A battery test shows it is tired.
causes2.fix: The battery and charging system are tested, then the battery is replaced or a corroded cable end is cleaned and tightened.

causes2.name: ABS or stability control module fault
causes2.tell: The light never clears, the scan tool struggles to talk to the ABS module, or codes point inside the unit itself.
causes2.fix: The control module or pump assembly is repaired or replaced, then set up for your car with a scan tool.

esp-bas-light.shop: A shop plugs in a scan tool that can talk to the ABS and stability modules, since a basic engine code reader usually cannot see these codes. They read the stored faults, check battery voltage, then watch each wheel speed sensor and the brake switch in live data, often on a short test drive. Expect roughly half an hour to an hour of diagnosis, more if the fault comes and goes or a wire has to be traced.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a service reminder, so there is nothing you are meant to reset. Clearing the code with a scan tool switches the light off for a moment, but the system turns it straight back on the next time it sees the same problem, often before you leave the parking lot. The one thing worth trying is the steering wheel relearn after a battery change: engine idling and car parked, turn the wheel fully left, fully right, back to center, then restart. If the light returns, the fault is still there and needs repairing.
reset.note: Some models need a scan tool to finish the steering angle calibration, and the exact steps differ by model and year.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the ESP BAS light on?
faqs.a: Days to a couple of weeks is usually fine if the car drives and brakes normally, but treat it as a job to book, not one to forget. Drive gently, leave extra room, and avoid fast corners. If the red brake light joins it, stop driving and get it towed.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the ESP BAS light on?
faqs.a: The ESP BAS light is not an emissions light, so it does not usually fail the computer part of an emissions test. It can still fail a safety inspection in states that have one, especially if the cause is a brake light switch and your brake lights do not work. Check what your state tests.

faqs.q: Does the ESP BAS light mean my brakes are failing?
faqs.a: Usually no. Your normal brakes work on their own and are not switched off by this light. But low brake fluid, very worn brakes or a bad brake light switch can all set it, so check the fluid level and have the brakes looked at.

faqs.q: Can the ESP BAS light go off by itself?
faqs.a: Yes, sometimes. If it came on because of a one-off voltage drop, a wheel spinning on ice or a steering sensor that lost its center, it can clear after a restart or a short drive and stay off. If it keeps coming back, something is genuinely broken and it needs codes read.

exhaust-emission-light.look: It lives in the main instrument cluster and is always amber or yellow. Most European makes draw a small engine block seen from the side with two or three curls of exhaust gas trailing off it; others use a short exhaust pipe with puffs of smoke. Several Asian makes draw nothing and simply write EMISSION SYSTEM or CHECK EXHAUST in the message screen.
exhaust-emission-light.flash: A flashing exhaust light means the engine is misfiring right now and unburned fuel is pouring into the catalytic converter, which can overheat it and start a fire. Pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. Don't keep driving; have it towed or checked before you go further.

diy.t: Tighten the fuel cap and check its seal
diy.how: A loose or cracked fuel cap lets fuel vapour escape and sets emissions faults on a lot of cars. Open the fuel door, take the cap off, and put it back on until it clicks. Look at the rubber ring for cracks or grit while it is in your hand. If that was the cause, the light often goes out on its own after a few drives.

diy.t: Get the trouble code read
diy.how: Write down every number it reports, P0420 and the rest. Those numbers tell a shop which part of the exhaust is complaining.
diy.tools: None, or a basic code reader

diy.t: Check the exhaust fluid level on a diesel
diy.how: If your diesel has a second, usually blue, filler cap next to the fuel filler, it uses exhaust fluid. Look at the dash readout for the level. Low fluid, or the wrong fluid in the tank, sets exhaust warnings on its own. Topping up from a sealed bottle of DEF or AdBlue is a job you can do standing at the filler.
diy.tools: A sealed bottle of DEF or AdBlue

diy.t: Listen for an exhaust leak
diy.how: With the car parked in park or neutral and the handbrake on, start it from cold and stand a few steps away from the front wheel. A ticking or puffing noise from beneath the front of the car often means a cracked pipe or a loose clamp, and air getting in there upsets the sensors. Do not touch any part of the exhaust: it is hot within a minute of starting.

diy.t: Look at the tailpipe smoke
diy.how: Start the car from cold and glance at the tailpipe from a few steps back. Thin white vapour on a cold morning is normal and clears as the engine warms. Thick black, blue, or sweet-smelling white smoke that does not clear is worth telling the shop about, because it narrows things down before the clock starts on diagnosis.

dont: Don't keep driving hard with the light flashing. A few miles of misfire can destroy a catalytic converter.
Don't clear the code and head straight to an emissions test. The car has to re-run its own self-checks and will fail as not ready.
Don't let a sensor fault sit for months. It very often takes the catalytic converter with it.
Don't assume it means the same as the check engine light on a European car. They are different warnings and both sets of codes need reading.

causes2.name: Oxygen (lambda) sensor
causes2.tell: The commonest cause. Fuel economy slips, the idle can be slightly rough, and the stored code names a sensor by bank and position. A shop compares the sensor's live reading with what the engine is actually doing to prove it is lying.
causes2.fix: Replace the sensor that has failed. A car has two or four of them and only the bad one gets changed.

causes2.name: Exhaust leak or loose clamp ahead of a sensor
causes2.tell: A ticking or puffing noise from the front of the exhaust, often loudest when cold. The extra air fools the sensors into reporting a lean mixture, so the car sets an emissions fault with nothing wrong with the sensor itself.
causes2.fix: Weld or replace the cracked section, or fit a new flange gasket and clamp.

causes2.name: EGR valve clogged with soot
causes2.tell: More common on diesels and turbocharged gas engines. Rough idle, hesitation pulling away, and a code about EGR flow. A shop can watch the valve stick part open or part shut on a scan tool.
causes2.fix: Clean or replace the EGR valve, and the cooler behind it if that is blocked too.

causes2.name: NOx sensor on a diesel
causes2.tell: Modern diesels only. The car often drops into reduced power and may warn that restarts will be blocked after so many miles. The code names the NOx sensor before or after the catalyst. These fail fairly often on European diesels.
causes2.fix: Replace the sensor. On many cars the new one has to be coded to the engine computer afterwards.

causes2.name: Worn out catalytic converter
causes2.tell: Usually follows months of an ignored sensor fault or misfire. A faint rotten-egg smell, sluggish acceleration, and the classic catalyst efficiency code P0420. A shop proves it by comparing the readings either side of the converter.
causes2.fix: Replace the converter, and fix whatever killed it first, or the new one dies the same way.

causes2.name: Misfire from spark plugs or ignition coils
causes2.tell: This is the flashing version of the light. The car shakes at idle, feels down on power, and the code names a cylinder. A shop swaps a coil to another cylinder to see whether the misfire follows it.
causes2.fix: Replace the failed coil or the spark plugs, usually as a full set.

exhaust-emission-light.shop: The shop plugs in a scan tool first and reads the stored codes along with the snapshot of data the car saved when the fault happened. Then it watches the oxygen and NOx sensor readings live with the engine running, checks how far the computer is trimming the fuel, and often smoke-tests the exhaust and intake for leaks before touching a single part. On a diesel they also look at the exhaust fluid, the EGR valve and the particulate filter. Expect about an hour of diagnosis, longer if the fault only shows up out on the road.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a service reminder, so there is nothing to reset. A scan tool will switch it off, but it comes back within a few drives until the real fault is repaired. Once the part is actually fixed the light goes out on its own, after the car has re-run its own emissions self-checks. That can take a few days of mixed driving rather than one trip round the block.
reset.note: Some makes will not clear the light until the car has completed a full drive cycle, which usually means a cold start plus some highway miles.

faqs.q: Is this the same as the check engine light?
faqs.a: On most American and Japanese cars, yes, because the check engine light covers emissions faults. Many European cars and a few Asian ones give the exhaust its own amber light so they can point you at the exhaust rather than the whole engine. If both are lit, have both sets of codes read.

faqs.q: Will my car pass an emissions test with this light on?
faqs.a: In most states that test, no. An emissions warning lit at the time of the test fails the plug-in part of the test whatever the tailpipe reads. Clearing the code on the way there does not help either, because the test also checks that the car has finished its own self-checks.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the exhaust emission light on?
faqs.a: If it is flashing, or the car has lost power, pull over when it's safe and turn the engine off. If it is steady and the car feels normal, drive gently and book a check within a week or two.

faqs.q: Why has the car suddenly lost power?
faqs.a: Modern cars deliberately cut power when the exhaust reports a fault, to protect the catalytic converter or the particulate filter. It is called limp or reduced power mode. It is not damage in itself, and full power comes back once the fault is repaired.

faqs.q: Does the light reset itself?
faqs.a: After a genuine repair, yes. The car runs its emissions self-checks over the next few trips and switches the light off when they pass, which can take a few days of mixed driving. If nothing has been repaired, it will come back every time.

glow-plug-light.look: An amber symbol in the cluster that looks like a coiled spring or a squiggly hot wire, usually drawn between two short upright lines. Diesel trucks from Ford, Ram and GM often skip the symbol and spell out WAIT TO START or WAIT instead. On VW, Mercedes and other European diesels it is the curly coil, and it sits near the other engine lights. It only appears on diesels. A plug symbol on an electric car or plug-in hybrid is a different light: it means a charging cable is connected.
glow-plug-light.flash: Flashing, or staying on after the engine is warm, is a fault. (A steady light for a few seconds before you start, or up to fifteen or twenty seconds on a freezing morning, is normal pre-heating.) On many European diesels the flashing version also means the engine has dropped into a reduced power mode to protect itself.

diy.t: Let the pre-heat finish before you crank
diy.how: Turn the key to on, or press the start button once without starting on a push-button diesel, and wait for the coil symbol to go out before you crank. In cold weather that can take fifteen or twenty seconds. Cranking before the light goes out is the number one cause of hard cold starting on a healthy diesel.

diy.t: Write down exactly what the engine does
diy.how: Note whether the light is steady or flashing, whether it only misbehaves when the engine is stone cold, how many seconds you have to crank, and whether you get white or grey smoke out the tailpipe for the first minute. A shop can narrow this down in half the time with those four answers, because no single symptom proves a glow plug on its own.

diy.t: Check the battery terminals and have the battery tested
diy.how: With the engine off and cold, look at the posts on top of the battery or batteries - diesels often have two. You want clean metal and clamps that will not move when you nudge them. White or blue fluff means a poor connection. Many parts stores can test a battery in the parking lot, and a tired battery makes a glow plug problem look far worse than it is.

diy.t: Read the owner's manual page for this light
diy.how: Look up the coil symbol or the WAIT TO START message in the index of your manual. Makes do not agree on what the flashing version means - on some it is only the glow plugs, on others the same lamp flashes for a general engine fault. Two minutes in the manual tells you which kind of car you have, and whether it says to limit how you drive.

dont: Don't crank for more than about ten seconds at a stretch - a diesel starter gets very hot. Wait a minute between tries.
Don't spray starting fluid or ether into a glow-plug diesel; it can crack a piston or bend a rod.
Don't tow or haul with the light flashing - on many diesels the flash means the engine has already cut its own power.
Don't just clear the code; the light comes back on the next cold start, because the computer retests the plugs every time.

causes2.name: One or more burned out glow plugs
causes2.tell: Hard starting when the engine has sat overnight, fine once it is warm, often with white or grey smoke and a rough shaky idle for the first half a minute. Usually stores a code naming the circuit, such as a glow plug circuit fault on cylinder two.
causes2.fix: The bad plugs are replaced, and most shops do the whole set at once because they all have the same age on them.

causes2.name: Failed glow plug relay or control module
causes2.tell: All of the plugs test fine but none of them ever heat up, so the engine is hard to start in cold weather every single time rather than now and then. Sometimes you can hear a click missing when the key goes on. Stores a control circuit code rather than one naming a cylinder.
causes2.fix: The relay or the small control box that feeds the plugs is replaced. Relays fail more often than the plugs themselves on some engines.

causes2.name: Corroded wiring or bus bar at the plugs
causes2.tell: The fault comes and goes, or only shows up after wet weather or a winter of road salt. One or two cylinders are reported as open while the rest are normal, and the trouble often moves between cylinders over time.
causes2.fix: The harness, connectors or the metal strip that links the plugs is cleaned up or replaced. On some engines this means getting past the intake to reach it.

causes2.name: Blown glow plug fuse or fusible link
causes2.tell: The symptom arrives suddenly and completely - the engine was fine yesterday and today it will not pre-heat at all. The scan reports the whole circuit as dead. A blown fuse is a symptom, so a good shop looks for what blew it.
causes2.fix: The fuse or link is replaced, and the circuit is tested to find whatever overloaded it, usually a shorted plug or a chafed wire.

causes2.name: Bad coolant or intake air temperature sensor
causes2.tell: The plugs and the module are all healthy, but the engine thinks it is already warm so it never runs a pre-heat cycle. The temperature gauge may read oddly, or the engine may also idle rough and use more fuel than usual.
causes2.fix: The sensor is replaced and the reading is checked against the real engine temperature on a scan tool.

causes2.name: An unrelated engine fault using the same lamp
causes2.tell: Mostly European diesels. The light flashes while you drive, the engine feels flat or down on power, and there is nothing at all wrong with the plugs. The stored code points somewhere else entirely, such as the exhaust gas valve or a pressure sensor.
causes2.fix: Whatever the stored code points at gets repaired.

glow-plug-light.shop: A shop reads the codes first, because the code usually says whether the problem is one cylinder or the whole circuit. Then, with the engine off, they measure each plug and watch how much current the system pulls when the key goes on - a dead plug draws nothing and a shorted one draws far too much. They also check power and ground at the relay or control box, and the battery, since weak batteries fake this fault. Allow about an hour, more on engines where the plugs sit under the intake.

reset.how: There is nothing here you are meant to reset. The steady light at key-on is the system working, and it goes out by itself. The flashing or stay-on version is a fault, and clearing the code only hides it - the computer tests the plugs again on the next cold start, so the light is back within a day or two. Fix the plug, relay or wiring and the light goes out on its own.
reset.note: Some diesels keep the fault stored until the engine has been through a cold start, so the light may take a day to clear after a correct repair.

faqs.q: Can I drive with the glow plug light on?
faqs.a: If the engine starts and runs smoothly, short local trips are usually fine, and the car will often behave normally once it is warm. Expect hard starting on cold mornings and a rough first minute. If the light is flashing, the engine feels down on power, or you get heavy white smoke, get it looked at before you drive much further.

faqs.q: Why does it only cause trouble in cold weather?
faqs.a: Glow plugs are only there to pre-warm the cylinders so diesel will light off when the engine is cold. Once the engine is warm it does not need them at all, which is why a car with dead plugs starts fine all summer and then refuses on the first frosty morning.

faqs.q: Do I have to replace all the glow plugs at once?
faqs.a: You don't have to, but most shops will. The plugs have all done the same mileage, so the others are usually close behind, and getting to them is most of the work.

faqs.q: Will a glow plug light fail an emissions test?
faqs.a: The light itself is not what testers look at. The problem is that a glow plug fault usually also sets a check engine light, and in states that plug into the computer a stored engine code fails the test. A diesel that smokes heavily on a cold start can also fail a visual or opacity check.

faqs.q: Can a bad glow plug damage the engine?
faqs.a: Not quickly, but it is not harmless either. Long cranking wears the starter and battery, and unburnt diesel washing past the rings dilutes the oil and can wear the engine over time. The worse risk is a plug tip breaking off inside a cylinder, which can damage the engine.

high-beam-light.look: A small blue symbol in the cluster, shaped like a headlamp lying on its side with four or five straight lines shooting out to the left. Blue means main beam almost everywhere. Cars that switch beams for you show a second version with a letter A or the word AUTO beside the lamp, often green or white, which only means the automatic mode is armed.
high-beam-light.flash: The blue symbol flicking on and off as you drive usually means you are holding the stalk in the flash to pass position, or that an automatic high beam system is dipping and raising the beams for traffic ahead. A symbol that flickers while nobody touches the stalk points instead to a worn headlight switch or a poor ground.

diy.t: Check the stalk is not left in the high beam position
diy.how: With the car parked and the headlights on, push the lever on the left of the steering wheel toward the dash and then pull it back. The blue symbol should come on and go off cleanly as you move it. If it stays lit in both positions, the switch inside that stalk is the likely problem and your beams really are up.

diy.t: See which beams are actually lit
diy.how: Park a few feet from a garage door or a plain wall at dusk, switch the main beams on and look at the reflection. Both sides should be bright and aimed much the same. One dim or dead side with the blue light still on means a burned out bulb, because the symbol follows the switch and not the bulbs.

diy.t: Check the cabin fuse for the headlights
