diy.how: The cabin fuse box is usually behind a cover at the end of the dash or below the glovebox, and the lid carries a map of what each fuse feeds. With the car switched off, find the fuse marked high beam or headlamp, pull it and look at the little metal strip inside. A broken strip means a blown fuse. Only ever replace it with the same number.
diy.tools: Owner's manual and a fuse puller

diy.t: Clean the camera glass if the car dips its own beams
diy.how: Automatic high beams watch the road through the same camera as lane keeping, up on the windshield behind the mirror. Clean that patch of glass inside and out and clear away snow or ice. A dirty or iced camera makes the car hold low beam, or flick between the two for no reason at all.
diy.tools: Glass cleaner and a soft cloth

dont: Don't leave main beams up in traffic; you blind the oncoming driver and in most states it is a ticket.
Don't touch a halogen bulb's glass with bare fingers, because skin oil makes it burn out early.
Don't drop an LED bulb into a housing built for halogen to chase more light; the beam scatters into other drivers' eyes.
Don't assume the blue symbol means both beams work, because one side can be dead with the light still on.

causes2.name: High beams are simply switched on
causes2.tell: The blue symbol goes on and off cleanly as you move the stalk, both beams are bright against a wall, and nothing else on the dash is lit. Nothing is wrong at all.
causes2.fix: Move the stalk back to low beam. No parts and no repair needed.

causes2.name: Burned out high beam bulb
causes2.tell: The symbol comes on as normal but only one side lights up bright against a wall. Many cars use a separate bulb, or a separate filament, for main beam, so low beams can look perfect while main beam is dead.
causes2.fix: The bulb is replaced, usually reached from inside the engine bay or through a cover in the wheel arch.

causes2.name: Worn headlight or multifunction switch
causes2.tell: The blue light stays on with the stalk in the low beam position, or main beam works only while you hold the stalk in the flash position. Wiggling the stalk changes what happens, which points at the switch rather than a bulb.
causes2.fix: The combination switch on the steering column is replaced, which means taking the column covers off.

causes2.name: Blown fuse or failed headlight relay
causes2.tell: Both main beams are dead together while the low beams work fine, and you may hear no click from the fuse box when you pull the stalk. A fuse with a broken strip inside tells the same story.
causes2.fix: The fuse or the relay is replaced. If the fuse blows again, a technician looks for the short that killed it.

causes2.name: Automatic high beam camera or module fault
causes2.tell: On a car that dips its own beams, it stops switching to main beam at all, or an assist warning lights up at the same time. Lane keeping often misbehaves with it, because both read the road through the camera on the windshield.
causes2.fix: The windshield camera or its wiring is repaired or replaced, then the camera is aimed again with a scan tool.

causes2.name: Corroded bulb socket, ground or wiring
causes2.tell: Main beam flickers, goes dim, or works only over bumps, and the plug at the back of the headlight looks green, brown or part melted when you look at it.
causes2.fix: The socket or the damaged length of wire and its ground point is repaired or replaced.

high-beam-light.shop: A shop does the simple checks first: switch the beams on, look at both headlights, then test the plug at the back of the dead lamp to see whether power is arriving. Power there and no light means a bulb or a corroded socket. No power means the switch, the relay, the fuse or the wiring, and they work backwards from the fuse box. On a car with automatic high beams they also scan the camera module for codes. Fifteen minutes to half an hour covers most of it.

reset.how: There is nothing to reset. The blue symbol is a plain indicator wired to the main beam circuit, so it is lit because the beams are up and it goes out the moment you dip them. If it stays on with the stalk down, that is a switch or wiring fault, and disconnecting the battery or clearing codes will change nothing, because the car does not store a code for this lamp in the first place.
reset.note: Automatic high beams do have their own on and off setting in the car's menus, but that is a setting, not a reset.

faqs.q: Why is the blue light on when I didn't turn the high beams on?
faqs.a: Either the stalk got nudged, or the switch inside it has worn and is stuck on main beam. Move the lever through both positions and watch the symbol. If it will not go out, your beams really are up and other drivers are being dazzled, so stay on low beam until the switch is fixed.

faqs.q: Is it illegal to drive with high beams on?
faqs.a: Every US state has a rule about dipping your beams for oncoming traffic and for cars you are following, usually within a few hundred feet. Leaving them up is a ticketable offence, and more to the point it blinds the driver coming the other way. Dip them as soon as you see headlights or tail lights.

faqs.q: My high beams don't work but the blue light comes on. Why?
faqs.a: The symbol is wired to the switch, not to the bulbs, so it lights up as soon as the car is told to use main beam whether anything shines or not. Both beams dead at once usually means a fuse or a relay. One side dead usually means a bulb or its plug.

faqs.q: Will this make me fail inspection?
faqs.a: The indicator itself is not an inspection item in most states, but your headlights are. A dead main beam or a beam aimed too high can fail a state safety inspection where one is done. Get the bulbs working and the aim checked, and the symbol takes care of itself.

lane-assist-light.look: This one sits in the main instrument cluster, usually a small car between two lane lines, or a car with one wheel crossing a line. Toyota and Lexus call it LTA or LDA, Honda calls it LKAS or road departure, and some cars show no symbol at all, just a text message such as front camera blocked or lane keeping unavailable.
lane-assist-light.flash: A flashing amber lane symbol is the system telling you right now that you are drifting out of your lane, usually with a beep or a buzz in the wheel or the seat. That is normal operation, not a fault. A symbol that sits there steady in amber, with no drifting, means the system is switched off or cannot see the road.

diy.t: Clean the glass in front of the camera
diy.how: Look up at the mirror from inside the car. The camera is the small black box stuck to the windshield just above or behind the mirror. Clean that patch of glass inside and out with glass cleaner and a soft cloth, and brush off any snow or ice from the outside. Many cars switch the warning off on their own within a minute or two of driving once the camera can see again.
diy.tools: Glass cleaner and a soft cloth

diy.t: Wipe the sensor area in the front grille
diy.how: Walk to the front of the parked car and look in the middle of the grille or the lower bumper for a smooth plastic panel or a badge shaped cover. That hides the radar. Wipe mud, slush, bugs and road salt off it with a damp cloth. Do not pry the cover off, and do not fit a plate frame or a badge in front of it.

diy.t: Check the system has not simply been switched off
diy.how: Most cars let you turn lane keeping off with a button near the steering wheel or in a touchscreen menu, and some then show a steady indicator to remind you. Look in the owner's manual index under lane keeping or driver assist, find the setting and check which way it is set. If someone turned it off, turning it back on clears the light.

diy.t: Look for new glass, stickers or a dash cam
diy.how: Anything new in front of the camera upsets it: a fresh windshield, a toll tag, a parking sticker, tint, a dash cam or a phone mount. Move whatever you can out of that square of glass above the mirror. A replaced windshield is different: the camera has to be aimed again on special equipment, and that is a shop job.

dont: Don't rely on the lane nudge or the warning beep while this light is on; assume the system will not help you at all.
Don't scrape ice off the camera area with a hard scraper or pour hot water on cold glass.
Don't fit stickers, tint, a dash cam or a phone mount in the square of glass in front of the camera.
Don't skip camera calibration after a windshield replacement just because the warning went out by itself.

causes2.name: Dirt, ice, snow or heavy rain blocking the camera or radar
causes2.tell: The light comes on in bad weather or after a slushy, salty drive, and the dash often shows a message about a blocked camera or sensor. It usually clears by itself once the glass and the grille are clean and dry.
causes2.fix: Cleaning the glass in front of the camera and the radar area behind the grille. No parts needed.

causes2.name: Windshield camera not aimed after new glass
causes2.tell: The light appeared within a day or two of a windshield replacement or a chip repair. The car may complain that the camera is blocked or misaligned even though the glass is spotless.
causes2.fix: A shop parks the car to measured targets and re-aims the camera with a scan tool, a job called calibration.

causes2.name: Front radar sensor failed or knocked out of line
causes2.tell: Usually turns up after a minor front end bump, a curb strike or a parking knock. Adaptive cruise will not set either, and the stored code points to the radar module not answering or reporting itself out of alignment.
causes2.fix: The radar unit behind the grille is re-aimed or replaced, then calibrated to the car.

causes2.name: Faulty windshield camera module
causes2.tell: The warning stays on with clean glass, clear weather and no recent bodywork or glass work. A scan tool shows the camera module itself reporting an internal fault rather than a blocked view.
causes2.fix: The camera assembly behind the mirror is replaced and then calibrated to the car.

causes2.name: Wiring, connector or fuse fault at the assist module
causes2.tell: Several helpers drop out at once, so lane keeping, collision warning and adaptive cruise all stop together, and the codes read as lost communication with a module rather than one sensor misbehaving.
causes2.fix: A technician traces the power, ground and network wiring to the module and repairs the bad connector, wire or fuse.

lane-assist-light.shop: A shop plugs in a scan tool and reads the codes the assist module stored, because the same amber symbol covers a dirty camera, a dead radar and a wiring fault. They look at the glass and the radar area, check live data from the camera, and road test the car if nothing obvious turns up. Expect the diagnosis to take about an hour. Calibration, if it is needed, is a separate job that takes targets, floor space and more time.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a reminder, so clearing the code fixes nothing. If the camera or radar was only blocked or dirty, the car switches the light off by itself once it can see again, often within a minute of driving. If a sensor, a module or its wiring has actually failed, the light comes straight back and keeps coming back until the part is repaired or replaced and, where the car calls for it, aimed again.
reset.note: Lane keeping can also be switched off on purpose in the car's menus, and on some makes that puts a steady indicator on the dash.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the lane assist light on?
faqs.a: In most US states a driver assist warning is not an inspection failure, because these systems are not part of emissions testing and are not on the state safety checklist. A few states and some commercial inspections do fail any lit warning lamp, so it is worth one phone call to the station first.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with this light on?
faqs.a: As long as you need to. The car steers, stops and accelerates exactly as before. What you lose is the backup: the lane nudge, the drift warning, and often collision warning and adaptive cruise too. Drive as though the car has none of them, because right now it does not.

faqs.q: Does the lane assist light reset itself?
faqs.a: Often, yes. If the cause was snow, slush, fog, heavy spray or a dirty windshield, the light goes out on its own once the camera can see the road again. If it is still there after the glass is clean and the weather is clear, something has failed and it needs a shop.

faqs.q: Is my car less safe at night with this light on?
faqs.a: A little. On many cars the same camera also runs automatic high beams and pedestrian detection, so those stop working too. Your headlights, brakes and steering are untouched. Treat the car as an older one with no electronic helpers and give yourself more room.

faqs.q: Does a new windshield really need the camera recalibrated?
faqs.a: Yes, on any car with a camera mounted on the glass. The camera has to know exactly where it is pointing to judge lane lines and distance, and new glass moves it. Ask the glass shop who does the calibration before the work starts, not after.

low-fuel-light.look: A small amber or yellow gas-pump symbol, usually tucked at the low end of the fuel gauge or just below it. Some cars light the last bar of the gauge instead, and some show a text line such as LOW FUEL or REFUEL SOON in the driver display. The little triangle or arrow next to the pump on the gauge is not part of the warning; it tells you which side of the car the filler door is on.

diy.t: Read the distance-to-empty number
diy.how: Most cars built in the last fifteen years show a range or miles-to-empty readout in the driver display. Scroll to it with the steering wheel buttons or the stalk and see what it says. Treat it as a rough guide only, because it is based on how you have been driving and it gets less accurate as the tank empties.

diy.t: Look up your reserve in the owner's manual
diy.how: The manual lists the tank size and often says how much fuel is left when the light comes on. Knowing your reserve tells you how much room you really have. Keep the figure in your head so you are not guessing the next time the light appears.

diy.t: Fill the tank and watch the gauge
diy.how: Fill up as you normally would, then start the car and look at the gauge. If the needle climbs to full and the light goes out, nothing is wrong and you simply ran low. If the gauge barely moves, stays on empty, or the light stays lit with a full tank, the problem is the sender in the tank or the gauge itself, not the fuel.

diy.t: Look for a fuel leak where you park
diy.how: With the car switched off, walk around it and look at the pavement for a wet patch or a rainbow sheen, and sniff for a strong gasoline smell. A leaking tank or line empties a tank far faster than normal and is a fire risk. If you see or smell fuel, do not drive it, and have it towed to a shop.

diy.t: Note the miles since your last fill-up
diy.how: Reset the trip odometer every time you fill up. If the light comes on after a normal number of miles for your car, the tank is genuinely low. If it comes on after only a short trip, the gauge or the sender is lying to you and you should have it looked at before you get stranded.

dont: Don't keep driving on fumes to stretch the tank; the pump sits in the fuel to stay cool and can overheat when it runs dry.
Don't trust the gauge if it has been jumping around or sticking; go by the miles you have driven since your last fill-up.
Don't pour anything but fuel into the tank, and never carry spare gasoline in a jug that isn't an approved fuel container.
Don't coast downhill in neutral to save fuel; on most cars it uses more, and you lose engine braking.

causes2.name: The tank really is low
causes2.tell: The needle is sitting near the E mark, the range readout is a small number, and the light came on after a normal amount of driving. It goes out on its own a minute or two after you fill up. This is the ordinary reason and it is by far the most common one.
causes2.fix: Add fuel.

causes2.name: Worn fuel level sender in the tank
causes2.tell: The gauge sticks on empty or on full, drops suddenly, or the light stays lit right after you fill the tank. The float arm and its resistor wear out with age. A scan usually finds a stored fuel level code such as P0461 or P0462.
causes2.fix: The sender sits inside the fuel tank, so the shop either reaches it through an access panel under the back seat or lowers the tank. On most cars the sender comes as part of the in-tank pump assembly.

causes2.name: In-tank fuel pump module has failed
causes2.tell: The gauge reads wrong and the car also struggles: long cranking before it starts, a stumble under hard acceleration, or a whine from the back of the car. The sender is built into the same unit as the pump, so one failure can cause both complaints.
causes2.fix: The whole pump and sender module is replaced as one piece, which means getting into or dropping the fuel tank.

causes2.name: Broken wire or corroded connector at the tank
causes2.tell: The gauge pegs all the way full or all the way empty, or it flickers when you go over a bump. The plug on top of the tank and the ground strap near it sit under the car and take road salt and water. A stored P0460 or P0463 points this way.
causes2.fix: The shop repairs the damaged wire, cleans or replaces the connector, and fixes the ground.

causes2.name: Instrument cluster or gauge fault
causes2.tell: Other needles misbehave at the same time, the gauges do not sweep when you first switch on, or the display flickers. The sender tests good when the shop measures it, which leaves the cluster. More common on higher-mileage cars with stepper-motor gauges.
causes2.fix: The cluster is either rebuilt by a specialist or replaced, and a replacement usually has to be programmed to the car and the mileage transferred.

low-fuel-light.shop: A shop starts by confirming how much fuel is actually in the tank, then plugs in a scanner and watches the fuel level sender's live reading while the tank is filled or drained. If the reading is flat, stuck, or jumps, they test the wiring and the plug on top of the tank before condemning anything inside it. Expect about half an hour for that check, longer if the tank has to come down to reach the sender.

reset.how: There is nothing to reset here. The low fuel light is simply reporting what the sender in the tank measures, and it switches itself off within a minute or two of filling up. If it stays lit with a full tank, the car is telling you about a real fault in the sender, the wiring or the gauge, and clearing the code with a scanner only hides it until the next drive.
reset.note: A few cars need one full fill-up before the miles-to-empty readout settles down again.

faqs.q: How far can I drive with the low fuel light on?
faqs.a: It varies a lot by car, so don't count on a set number. Your owner's manual or the miles-to-empty display gives the real figure for your car. Treat the reserve as a cushion to reach a station, not a target. Hills, towing, cold weather and a nearly empty tank all cut it short.

faqs.q: Why is my low fuel light on with a full tank?
faqs.a: That is not a fuel problem, it is a measuring problem. The float-and-resistor sender inside the tank, the wiring to it, or the gauge in the dash is giving a false reading. Have it scanned, because until it is fixed you have no reliable idea how much fuel you have.

faqs.q: Will a low fuel light fail an inspection?
faqs.a: No. It is an information light, not an emissions or safety fault, so no state fails a car for it. A check engine light stored alongside it, for example a fuel level sensor code, can cause a failure in states that read the car's computer.

faqs.q: Is it bad to always run the tank down to the light?
faqs.a: It shortens the life of the fuel pump. The pump sits down in the fuel and uses it to stay cool, so running the tank low repeatedly makes it work hot. Sediment that settles at the bottom of an older tank also gets picked up more easily.

faqs.q: What happens if I actually run out of fuel?
faqs.a: The engine sputters, loses power and stops, and you lose power steering and power brake assist while the car is still rolling, so steering and stopping take much more effort. Get to the shoulder as soon as you feel it stumble. Adding a gallon or two is usually all it takes to restart, though some diesels need bleeding.

oil-pressure-light.look: A red symbol low in the instrument cluster, often near the temperature gauge, shaped like an old-fashioned oil can tipped forward with a single drop falling from the spout. Some makes add a short wavy line beneath the drop. Others show no symbol and print LOW OIL PRESSURE in the driver display. Watch the color: the same oil can in amber usually means a low oil level or a service reminder, not lost pressure.
oil-pressure-light.flash: On some cars the light flickers or blinks instead of staying on, typically at idle, when braking or going round a bend. That pattern often means the oil level is low enough that the pump briefly sucks air as the oil sloshes away from the pickup, though a failing pump or sensor can do it too. It is still a stop-and-check light, not a glitch, and it usually turns solid if you keep driving.

diy.t: Check the oil level on the dipstick
diy.how: Park on level ground, switch the engine off and wait about five minutes for the oil to drain back down. Pull the dipstick out, wipe it clean, push it fully home, then pull it again and read where the oil film ends. It should sit between the two marks or inside the crosshatched area. If no oil shows on the stick at all, the level is dangerously low and the engine must not be restarted.

diy.t: Add the correct oil if the level is low
diy.how: Find the grade in your owner's manual or on the oil filler cap, something like 5W-30 or 0W-20, and buy that. With the engine off and cool, unscrew the filler cap on top of the engine and pour in about a quart, wait two minutes, then re-check the dipstick. Repeat until the level reaches the upper mark and stop there, because overfilling causes its own problems.

diy.t: Look for where the oil went
diy.how: Walk around the car and look at the ground where it has been parked for fresh dark wet patches. With the engine off and cool, look over the top of the engine for oil streaks or a wet filler cap. Then think back: has the exhaust been smoking blue, and when was the last oil change? A car that is losing or burning oil will empty itself again within weeks, so the leak matters as much as the top-up.

diy.t: Look at the oil itself and listen to the engine
diy.how: On the dipstick, clean oil is amber to brown. Black and gritty means it is badly overdue. Milky or the color of a coffee milkshake means coolant is mixing in, which is a shop job today. Also recall what you heard before the light came on: a deep knocking, rattling or tapping from the engine means internal damage may already have started, and the car should be towed rather than driven.

dont: Don't drive on to get home or to reach a shop. Engine damage from lost oil pressure starts in seconds, so have it towed.
Don't keep restarting the engine to see whether the light clears. Every start with no pressure grinds the bearings a little more.
Don't mistake this red light for the amber oil change reminder. Red means the oil is not reaching the moving parts right now.
Don't top up with whatever oil is in the garage if you are unsure of the grade, and never pour engine oil into the transmission or steering filler.

causes2.name: Low oil level from a leak or from burning oil
causes2.tell: The dipstick reads below the low mark or shows nothing at all. There may be dark patches on the driveway, oil streaks around the engine, or blue smoke from the exhaust. The light often flickers in corners or at idle first, before it stays on.
causes2.fix: Top up to the correct level, then have the leak or the oil burning traced.

causes2.name: Faulty oil pressure sensor or switch
causes2.tell: The oil level is correct, the oil is fresh, the engine sounds completely normal and nothing smells hot. The light may come on and go off for no clear reason. Stored codes are usually in the P0520 to P0524 group. A shop confirms it by fitting a mechanical gauge in place of the sensor.
causes2.fix: The sensor is unscrewed from the engine and replaced.

causes2.name: Very overdue oil change or the wrong oil grade
causes2.tell: Service history shows the oil has gone far past its interval, or a thinner oil than the manual calls for was used. The oil on the dipstick is black and may smell burnt. The light tends to show at idle or when the engine is fully hot and the oil is at its thinnest.
causes2.fix: An oil and filter change with the exact grade the manufacturer specifies. If pressure returns and stays, nothing else is needed, but sludge may already have done damage.

causes2.name: Oil pickup screen clogged with sludge
causes2.tell: Normally found on an engine with a long history of missed oil changes. The level reads fine but the light is on, and pressure measured with a gauge is genuinely low. Often there is sludge visible around the filler cap.
causes2.fix: The oil pan is removed, the pickup tube and screen are cleaned or replaced, and the engine is flushed.

causes2.name: Failing oil pump
causes2.tell: Pressure measured on a mechanical gauge is low with a correct oil level and fresh oil. There may be a faint whine or ticking from the engine that rises with speed. Pressure is often lowest when hot and at idle.
causes2.fix: The pump is replaced.

causes2.name: Worn engine bearings or internal wear
causes2.tell: Usually a high-mileage engine, or one that ran low on oil at some point. There is a deep knocking or rumble that gets louder as you press the gas, and the light may clear briefly after a top-up before returning. Measured pressure is low across the board.
causes2.fix: This is an engine rebuild or a replacement engine, not a repair to one part.

oil-pressure-light.shop: The first thing a good shop does is confirm whether the pressure is really low or the sensor is lying. They check the oil level and condition, pull any stored codes, then unscrew the pressure sensor and fit a mechanical gauge in its place, reading pressure cold, hot and at several engine speeds against the manufacturer's spec. Along the way they look for leaks and listen for bearing noise. That testing is usually under an hour. If pressure is genuinely low, the next step is dropping the oil pan to inspect the pickup and pump, which is a much bigger job.

reset.how: There is nothing here that is meant to be reset. This light is a live reading from a sensor on the running engine, not a mileage reminder, so it goes out by itself the moment real oil pressure comes back. If you clear codes or disconnect the battery and the light returns as soon as the engine starts, that is the system working correctly and telling you the problem has not been fixed. Topping up oil to the right level is the only thing a driver can do that legitimately makes this light go out, and if it stays on after that, the engine should be towed rather than driven.
reset.note: Don't confuse this with the oil change or service reminder, which is a mileage counter and is designed to be reset after the service.

faqs.q: Can I drive a short distance with the oil pressure light on?
faqs.a: No, not even a mile. Without oil pressure the engine's bearings run metal on metal, and serious damage can happen in under a minute of running. Pull over somewhere safe, shut the engine off, and check the oil level. If the light comes back on with a correct oil level, have the car towed.

faqs.q: I added oil and the light is still on. What now?
faqs.a: Shut the engine off and stop driving it. A correct oil level with the light still lit means either the sensor has failed or the oil genuinely is not getting through, and you cannot tell which from the driver's seat. Only a mechanical pressure gauge fitted in place of the sensor answers that, so it needs to go to a shop on a truck.

faqs.q: Is the oil pressure light the same as the oil change light?
faqs.a: No, and it is the most costly mix-up on the dashboard. The oil change or service reminder is amber or yellow, often spelled out in words, and simply counts miles since the last service. The red oil can means pressure has dropped right now and the engine needs to be switched off.

faqs.q: Why does the oil light come on only at idle or in corners?
faqs.a: That pattern nearly always means the oil level is low. At idle the pump turns slowly and produces the least pressure, and in a corner the remaining oil slides away from the pump's pickup so it briefly draws air. Check the dipstick first, and expect the light to become constant if you keep driving on a low level.

faqs.q: Will this light pass a state inspection?
faqs.a: A lit red oil pressure warning may fail a safety inspection in states that check dashboard warning lights. More to the point, you should not be driving it to the test station in the first place.

parking-brake-light.look: It sits in the main cluster right in front of you, usually in the row of red lights near the temperature and oil lamps. Most cars show a red circle with a P inside and two small curved brackets on each side. Some use an exclamation mark in the circle instead, and some older cars just light the red word BRAKE. On many makes it is the very same lamp used for brake system faults.
parking-brake-light.flash: On some cars with a button-operated parking brake, the red light blinks instead of staying steady. A blinking light means the brake has not finished clamping or has not fully let go, so the car may not be held safely. Set it again, and if it keeps blinking, do not rely on it to hold the car on a slope.

diy.t: Release the brake fully and watch the light
diy.how: With the car parked and your foot on the brake pedal, push the parking brake pedal or button all the way down, or drop the hand lever flat against the floor or console. Watch the red light while you do it. If it goes out, that was all it was. If it is a hand lever, lift it and drop it once more: the switch under the lever can stick partway.

diy.t: Look at the brake fluid level
diy.how: With the engine off and cool, open the hood and find the small see-through plastic tank near the back of the engine bay on the driver's side, usually marked with a circle and exclamation mark cap. Shine a light through the side and look for the MIN and MAX marks. Do not open the cap. If the fluid sits at or below MIN, that is why the light is on and it needs a shop.

diy.t: Check whether a rear wheel is dragging
diy.how: If the light stayed on, drive a few minutes at low speed around your street, then park. Stand beside each rear wheel and hold the back of your hand a few inches from the wheel without touching the brake parts. If one side throws off much more heat than the other, or you smell something hot, the parking brake is still partly clamped and the car should not be driven far.

diy.t: Read what your own car calls the light
diy.how: Open the owner's manual, or search the PDF version on your phone, for the warning light pages. Makes use this one red lamp for different things, and the manual tells you whether yours covers the parking brake only or the whole brake system. It also says whether a steady light and a blinking light mean different things on your car.

dont: Don't drive with the lever or pedal partly engaged: it overheats and wears out the rear brakes.
Don't keep driving to see if it clears when the light stays on with the brake released.
Don't just keep topping up the brake fluid to make the light go out: the fluid is going somewhere.
Don't park on a slope trusting the handbrake if the light blinks or the lever pulls up with no resistance.

causes2.name: Parking brake left partly on, or a sticking switch
causes2.tell: The light goes out when you lift and firmly re-release the lever or pedal, or it flickers over bumps. A shop can watch the switch signal while moving the lever and see it stay closed when the brake is actually off.
causes2.fix: Adjust or replace the small switch at the base of the lever or pedal.

causes2.name: Low brake fluid from worn brake pads
causes2.tell: Fluid sits at or below the MIN line with no wet spots anywhere, and the pads look thin through the wheel. Often comes with a squeal or a grinding noise when you brake.
causes2.fix: Replace the worn pads, and the rotors if they are grooved or too thin, then set the fluid back to the full mark.

causes2.name: Brake fluid leak at a line, hose or caliper
causes2.tell: Fluid keeps dropping, the pedal feels soft or sinks slowly, and there is a damp or shiny spot on a wheel, behind a tire or under the master cylinder. This one is a safety problem, not a maintenance item.
causes2.fix: Replace the leaking hose, steel line, caliper or master cylinder, then bleed the brakes and refill the system.

causes2.name: Seized or stretched parking brake cable
causes2.tell: The lever pulls up much further than it used to, or it will not come back down, and the car still rolls when the brake is set. Common on cars that live in salt and snow.
causes2.fix: Replace the rusted or stretched cable and adjust the parking brake, including the rear shoes on cars that use them.

causes2.name: Faulty brake fluid level sensor
causes2.tell: The light is on but the fluid is right up at the full mark and the pedal feels normal. It often comes and goes with the fluid sloshing on corners.
causes2.fix: Replace the level sensor, which is part of the reservoir cap or clipped into the side of the tank.

parking-brake-light.shop: A shop starts by releasing the brake and watching the light, then checks the fluid level and the switch at the lever or pedal with a meter. If the fluid is low they look at every pad, hose and caliper for a leak. They will also pull codes from the brake and body modules, because some cars light this lamp from the ABS side. Plan on about half an hour to an hour before they can tell you what it is.

reset.how: This is not a reminder you reset after a service. It is a live warning, so it goes out on its own the moment the parking brake is fully off and the brake system reads as normal. Clearing it with a scan tool or pulling a fuse does nothing: it comes straight back until the switch, the fluid level or the leak behind it is actually repaired.
reset.note: A few cars keep the lamp on until the key is cycled off and on after the fault is fixed.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive with the parking brake light on?
faqs.a: If the light goes out as soon as you fully release the brake, yes. If it stays on with the brake released, treat it as a brake system warning and get it checked before you drive again, because the usual cause is low fluid. A soft or sinking pedal means stop and call for a tow.

faqs.q: Why is my parking brake light on when the brake is off?
faqs.a: Two common reasons. The little switch at the lever or pedal is stuck and still telling the car the brake is set, or the brake fluid has dropped below the minimum mark and the car is using the same red lamp to warn you. Checking the fluid level tells you which one you have.

faqs.q: I drove a few miles with the handbrake on. Did I damage anything?
faqs.a: A short, slow drive usually just glazes the rear brake pads and makes a burning smell for a while. Longer or faster driving can overheat the rear brakes and warp the rotors, and on cars with rear drums it can ruin the shoes. If the car pulls, smells hot or one rear wheel is much hotter than the other, have the rear brakes looked at.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with this light on?
faqs.a: In states that inspect brakes or check the dashboard, a red brake warning light on is normally a fail. If the light is on only because the handbrake was set, releasing it fixes the problem. If it stays on, expect to repair the cause before the car passes.

faqs.q: Does the parking brake light reset itself?
faqs.a: Yes, when the real cause is gone. It is a live warning, not a service reminder, so it switches off by itself once the brake is fully released and the fluid level and brake circuits read normal. There is no button or sequence to reset it.

seat-belt-light.look: A red figure sitting in a seat with a diagonal strap across the chest, usually in the middle of the instrument cluster or in the top row of lights. Some makes draw just the belt and buckle with no person, and some skip the symbol and put FASTEN SEAT BELT or BELT in the driver display. Newer cars often show a row of small seat outlines, one per seat, so you can see which passenger is the problem.
seat-belt-light.flash: On most cars the symbol flashes rather than glowing steadily, and a chime goes with it. The flashing and chiming usually get faster or louder once you pass about ten to fifteen miles per hour, and many cars repeat the reminder in bursts for a minute or two rather than nagging forever. A flashing reminder means the same thing as a steady one: a belt the car expects to be latched is not latched.

diy.t: Unlatch and re-latch every belt
diy.how: Pull each belt out, push the metal tongue into the buckle until you hear a solid click, then tug on the belt to make sure it holds. A tongue that is only half in will look latched but will not switch the reminder off. Do the driver and front passenger first, then the back seats, because many newer cars watch those too.

diy.t: Clear out the buckle slot
diy.how: Shine a phone light into the slot on the buckle and look for a coin, a crumb, a bit of wrapper or dried soda. Turn the buckle over and shake it, or puff it out with canned air. Do not jam anything metal into the slot; a wooden toothpick is enough to lift debris out of the opening.

diy.t: Empty the front passenger seat
diy.how: The passenger reminder is triggered by weight on the seat, so a laptop bag, a case of water, a toolbox or a bag of groceries can set it off. Move everything to the floor or the trunk and switch the car off and back on. If the light clears, the seat was simply being read as a person.

diy.t: Take off aftermarket belt covers and clips
diy.how: Padded shoulder covers, clip-on comfort adjusters and the dummy tongues sold to silence the chime all confuse the system, and some of them hold the buckle switch in the wrong position. Remove anything that was not fitted at the factory and try again. They also stop the belt from doing its job in a crash.

diy.t: Check what your car actually monitors
diy.how: Look up the reminder in the owner's manual index. It tells you whether your car watches only the front seats or the rear ones as well, how long the chime is meant to last, and whether a reminder appears when a rear passenger unbuckles mid-trip. That saves you hunting for a fault that is not there.

dont: Don't plug a dummy buckle or belt-silencer clip into the latch to kill the chime; it leaves whoever sits there unrestrained in a crash.
Don't ignore a reminder that stays on with everyone buckled, because the same circuit decides whether the front passenger air bag fires.
Don't take the seat or the buckle apart yourself; the belt system has an explosive tensioner built into it that can fire while you work.
Don't move a child seat to the front to quiet the reminder; the back seat is the safer place for it.

causes2.name: A belt that is not latched all the way
causes2.tell: The reminder goes out as soon as you push the tongue in harder and hear a second click, and it only ever happens with one particular seat. Often the belt has been shut in the door or twisted so the tongue cannot seat fully. This is the ordinary reason and the first thing to rule out.
causes2.fix: Re-latch the belt properly. Nothing to buy, and no shop visit needed unless it keeps happening.

causes2.name: Dirt, a coin or spilled drink in the buckle
causes2.tell: The tongue feels gritty going in, needs extra force, or will not click at all. Very common in family cars and in the seats children use. The reminder may come and go depending on how hard the belt is pushed in.
causes2.fix: The buckle is cleaned out. If the latch mechanism inside is sticky or damaged, the whole buckle assembly is replaced instead, which is a short job on a front seat.

causes2.name: Failed switch inside the buckle
causes2.tell: The light stays on with the belt firmly latched, or it goes out if you press the latched belt sideways. A proper restraint scan stores a buckle switch code. Age and the switch being flexed thousands of times are the usual causes.
causes2.fix: The buckle and its built-in switch are replaced as one assembly.

causes2.name: Passenger seat occupant sensor has failed
causes2.tell: The passenger reminder stays on with the seat completely empty, or the passenger air bag on and off indicator behaves oddly at the same time. A restraint scan stores an occupant classification code. More common on cars past about ten years old, where the pressure mat under the seat cover cracks.
causes2.fix: The sensor mat or its control module under the seat is replaced and the system is then recalibrated with a factory-level scan tool.

causes2.name: Damaged or unplugged wiring under the seat
causes2.tell: The light comes and goes as the seat is slid forward and back, or it first appeared right after a car seat was fitted, the carpet was cleaned, or something heavy was pushed under the seat. The harness under a front seat gets flexed every time the seat moves.
causes2.fix: The shop traces the harness, repairs the chafed wire or reconnects the plug that was knocked loose, and clears the stored code.

causes2.name: Restraint control module fault
causes2.tell: The belt reminder is lit together with the air bag warning, and a scan pulls several restraint codes at once rather than one. Can follow a minor collision, a flat battery, or water getting into the module's floor location.
causes2.fix: The module is tested, then repaired or replaced and programmed to the car. A module that recorded a crash has to be replaced rather than reset.

seat-belt-light.shop: From there they look at which seat the car is complaining about, watch the buckle switch change state as the belt is latched and unlatched, and check what the passenger seat sensor is reporting with the seat empty and with weight on it. That much usually takes half an hour to an hour. It runs longer if the seat cushion has to come apart to reach a sensor or a harness.

reset.how: This is not a light you are meant to reset. In normal use it goes out by itself the moment the belts the car is watching are latched, so there is no service procedure to run. When it stays on because of a fault, erasing the code with a scanner only turns the light off until the next time you start the car, and the fault comes straight back. The restraint system rechecks itself every start-up.
reset.note: Some makes publish a way to shorten or mute the chime, but that leaves a genuine fault unrepaired and the warning light lit.

faqs.q: Will a seat belt light fail a state inspection?
faqs.a: The reminder on its own is not usually an inspection item, but the belts themselves are, and a lit air bag or restraint warning does fail in a number of states. Since a stuck reminder often comes from the same restraint system, get it diagnosed before you book an inspection. Rules differ from state to state, so check yours.

faqs.q: Why is the light on when nobody is in the passenger seat?
faqs.a: Your car weighs that seat to decide whether someone is sitting there. A bag, a box or a pet is enough to set it off, and so is a cracked sensor mat under the seat cover. Clear the seat first; if the light stays on with an empty seat, the sensor or its wiring needs looking at.

faqs.q: Is the seat belt light connected to my air bags?
faqs.a: Yes. The same restraint module reads the buckle switches and the passenger seat sensor, and it uses that information to decide how hard to fire the air bags and whether to fire the passenger one at all. That is why a stuck reminder is worth fixing rather than living with.

faqs.q: Can I just turn the chime off?
faqs.a: Some makes have a procedure in the owner's manual or a dealer setting that shortens or disables it. It silences the noise without repairing anything, the warning light normally stays lit, and on a car where the reminder is faulty you have then hidden a restraint system problem. Not worth it.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with it on?
faqs.a: If it is on because a belt is undone, fix that before you move. If everyone is buckled and it is still lit, the car is drivable, but drive it knowing the restraint system has a fault and may not protect the front passenger properly. Book it in rather than leaving it for months.

security-light.look: A small amber or red symbol in the instrument cluster, often low down near the fuel gauge or off to one side. Most makes draw a car outline with a padlock over it; Toyota, Nissan and Hyundai often show a car with a key inside it instead. Older GM trucks and cars simply spell out the word SECURITY, and a few Hondas use a plain green key outline.
security-light.flash: A slow, steady blink once every second or two while the car is locked and switched off is normal - that is the anti-theft system standing guard. A fast blink, or a light that stays solid once you turn the key on, is the car telling you it cannot read the key, and that is when it usually will not start.

diy.t: Try your spare key
diy.how: Get the other key or fob and try starting the car with it. If the spare works, the problem is in the key you were using - a worn chip or a dead battery inside it. If neither key works, the fault is in the car and not the keys, which is useful to know before anyone sells you a new key.

diy.t: Replace the battery in the key fob
diy.how: Most fobs pop open along a seam with a coin or a small flat screwdriver and take one flat coin battery. Note which side faces up before you take the old one out, put the new one in the same way, and snap the fob back together. A weak fob battery is the single most common reason a car stops recognising its key.

diy.t: Hold the key against the start button or column
diy.how: Take the key off the ring and move your phone, wallet and any other fobs away from it. Press the key or fob flat against the start button, or against the plastic around the ignition on a car with a turn key, then try to start. Cars keep a backup reader there for exactly this situation.

diy.t: On some GM cars: let the car relearn the key
diy.how: On some GM cars, leaving the key in the on position lets the security system accept the key again. Sit in the car, turn the key to on without cranking, and leave it there for ten to fifteen minutes while the security light does its thing. When the light stops blinking, switch off, wait a minute, then try to start. On other makes this does nothing and can run down a weak battery, so check your owner's manual first.

diy.t: Look at the battery terminals
diy.how: With the engine off and cold, open the hood and look at the two posts on top of the battery. You want clean metal and clamps that do not move when you nudge them by hand. White or blue fluff, or a clamp you can wiggle, means poor voltage, and a security system that is short on volts will refuse the key. Have a shop clean and tighten them.

dont: Don't crank it over and over - you'll flatten the battery, and many systems lock you out for several minutes after a few failed attempts.
Don't buy a new key before the car has been scanned; the fault is in the car just as often as in the key.
Don't rely on the car for a long trip if it starts only after a few tries - the next time it may not restart at all.
Don't try to bypass or hot-wire the system; on most modern cars that just adds another module fault.

causes2.name: Weak or dead key fob battery
causes2.tell: The remote lock and unlock buttons stop working from a distance, or only work right next to the car. The car may still start if you hold the key against the start button. No fault codes stored, or a stored code about the key not being read.
causes2.fix: A new coin battery in the fob. A parts store or hardware store has them, and the shop will put one in while you wait.

causes2.name: Worn or damaged transponder key
causes2.tell: One key works and the other does not, or the key only works if you hold it at a certain angle. Often follows the key being dropped, washed or carried loose in a pocket for years. A scan shows the car is not receiving a key signal.
causes2.fix: A new key is cut and then programmed to your car so it is the only one that will start it.

causes2.name: Weak 12-volt battery or corroded terminals
causes2.tell: Slow cranking, dim dash lights, several warning lights on at once, or the trouble starts after the car sat for a few days. Often shows up on a cold morning and clears once the car is jump started.
causes2.fix: The battery is tested, and either the terminals are cleaned and tightened or the battery is replaced.

causes2.name: Faulty antenna ring or key reader
causes2.tell: Both keys fail, and the car cranks but will not fire, or fires and dies after a second or two. A scan tool shows no key signal at all even with a known good key. Common on cars with a turn key and high mileage on the ignition.
causes2.fix: The ring or reader around the ignition or start button is replaced and the keys are matched to it again.

causes2.name: Ignition lock cylinder or anti-theft sensor fault
causes2.tell: The key feels loose or sticky in the ignition, or the light comes on only when you hit a bump or turn the wheel. Very common on older GM cars and trucks that use a sensor in the lock rather than a chip in the key.
causes2.fix: The lock cylinder and its sensor are replaced and the car is taught the new part, which takes a wait of up to half an hour on some cars.

causes2.name: Immobilizer or body control module failure
causes2.tell: Both keys fail, the battery and wiring check out, and a scan shows the module itself not answering or reporting an internal fault. Sometimes starts after the car has been in water, or after someone else replaced a computer on it.
causes2.fix: The module is replaced and then programmed to your car and your keys, which needs dealer-level equipment on most makes.

security-light.shop: They check battery voltage, then watch live data to see whether the car is picking up the key at all, and wiggle the wiring at the base of the steering column while they watch. From there it is a test of the reader, the module and each key. Expect about an hour, longer if the fault comes and goes.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a reminder, so there is nothing you are meant to reset. Clearing the code with a scan tool wipes the light for a moment, but the car still does not trust the key, so it comes straight back - usually the next time you shut the engine off. There is a real key relearn procedure, but it belongs at the end of a repair, after the bad key, reader or module has been replaced.
reset.note: The relearn is different on every make, and on many cars it needs equipment only a dealer or a car locksmith has.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the security light on?
faqs.a: On its own the security light is not part of an emissions test, so in most states it does not fail you. The trouble is that a car which will not start cannot be tested at all, and some of these faults also switch on the check engine light, which does fail the test in states that read the computer.

faqs.q: Can I keep driving with the security light on?
faqs.a: If the engine starts and runs normally, short local trips are usually possible, but treat it as a warning that the next start is not guaranteed. Don't head out of town or park somewhere you can't be towed from. If the car starts and then shuts off on its own, stop using it and get it looked at.

faqs.q: Does the security light reset itself?
faqs.a: Sometimes. If it came on because the fob battery was fading or the car was low on voltage, it often clears on its own once that is fixed. If it keeps coming back, something in the system is failing and it will not sort itself out.

faqs.q: Why does my car start and then die a second later?
faqs.a: That is the anti-theft system doing its job. The engine is allowed to fire, then the computer cuts the fuel because it never got the right code back from the key. It points at the key, the reader around the ignition, or the module - not at the engine itself.

faqs.q: Can a locksmith make a new key, or do I need the dealer?
faqs.a: Usually, and a mobile car locksmith can often cut and program a key at your house, which saves a tow. Check that they handle your make, because some newer cars and most push-button keys still need dealer equipment.

slip-indicator-light.look: Both are amber words rather than drawn symbols, in the message area near the speedometer. Nissan uses the single word SLIP, with VDC OFF below or beside it; some models add a small skidding-car outline, and Infiniti often uses that car symbol with OFF next to it. Seeing SLIP and VDC OFF lit together is normal for this fault, and the ABS light frequently joins them.
slip-indicator-light.flash: A blinking SLIP light while you are driving is normal and means the system is actively catching a slipping wheel, so ease off the accelerator: the road is slicker than it looks. Nissan's manual says it also blinks for wheel spin when VDC has been switched off. A SLIP light that stays on steady is the warning, not the flashing one.

diy.t: Check the VDC OFF button
diy.how: Hunt for a button marked VDC OFF, usually low on the dash to the left of the steering wheel or near the shifter. It is easy to catch with a knee or a bag. Press it once with the car parked and the engine running, then shut the car off and restart. If both lights go out and stay out, the system was simply switched off. On 4WD models, check you are not still in 4LO, which turns VDC off on purpose.

diy.t: Do the ten-minute relearn drive
diy.how: If the lights came on after a battery change, a jump start or a battery that went flat, the system has lost its straight-ahead reference. Nissan's own instruction is to drive straight on a quiet, level road at more than about 10 mph for at least ten minutes. If the lights go out during that drive, nothing is broken. If they are still on at the end, there is a real fault to find.

diy.t: Check the tires and the spare
diy.how: Set all four tires to the pressure on the sticker in the driver's door opening, with the car cold. Then look at them: they should be the same size and brand, with similar tread depth. A space-saver spare or one odd tire makes that wheel turn at a different speed, which is enough to upset the system and light these warnings.

diy.t: Look at the brake fluid and pads
diy.how: With the engine off and cool, read the brake fluid level through the small see-through tank at the back of the engine bay: it should sit between the MIN and MAX marks. Nissan's manual notes that badly worn or non-standard brake pads, rotors or calipers can bring the VDC OFF light on. Peer through the wheel spokes at the pad: if the friction material looks paper thin, book a brake check.

diy.t: Check the battery terminals and restart
diy.how: With the engine off, look at the two battery terminals. They should be clean and tight, with no white or green crust and no movement when you nudge the cable by hand. Low voltage sets several warning lights at once on these cars. Start the car again and see whether the lights come back; if they clear but keep returning, have the battery tested, which many parts stores can do.

dont: Don't press the VDC OFF button just to make the warning go away; that only switches off the system that keeps you straight in a skid.
Don't stay on a space-saver or odd-size spare any longer than you must, it can trigger these lights on its own.
Don't ignore a SLIP light that's on with the check engine light; fix the engine fault first, because VDC shuts itself down when the engine computer has trouble.
Don't trust a light that keeps clearing and returning. Have the codes read instead of waiting for it to settle.

causes2.name: VDC switched off by the button or 4LO
causes2.tell: Only VDC OFF is lit, or VDC OFF with SLIP, the car is otherwise perfectly normal, and a scan tool finds no stored faults. Pressing the button or shifting out of 4LO puts the lights out.
causes2.fix: Nothing to fix. Press the VDC OFF button back on, or take the transfer case out of low range, and restart the car.

causes2.name: Wheel speed sensor or its wiring
causes2.tell: The ABS light is on too, the speedometer may flicker as you roll to a stop, and the code names one specific wheel. Rust, road salt or a wire rubbed through near the wheel are common on older Altimas, Pathfinders and Frontiers.
causes2.fix: The wheel comes off and that corner's sensor is replaced, or the damaged section of wiring is repaired.

causes2.name: Steering angle sensor needing a relearn or failed
causes2.tell: The lights began right after a battery change, jump start, alignment or steering work, and the ten-minute straight-line drive does not clear them. Codes mention the steering angle sensor.
causes2.fix: A shop relearns the sensor with a scan tool. If the sensor itself is bad it is replaced in the steering column and then calibrated.

causes2.name: Weak battery or bad battery connection
causes2.tell: A handful of warning lights came on at once, often after a slow crank or a few days parked, and they clear after a drive then return. A battery test shows it is worn out or a cable end is corroded.
causes2.fix: The battery and charging system are tested, then the battery is replaced or the corroded connection is cleaned and tightened.

causes2.name: An engine fault that shuts VDC down
causes2.tell: The check engine light is on with SLIP and VDC OFF, and the car may idle rough, hesitate or feel flat. VDC leans on engine power control, so the system switches off when the engine computer stores a fault.
causes2.fix: The engine fault is diagnosed and repaired, for example an ignition coil, a sensor or a misfire. The SLIP and VDC OFF lights go out once the engine code is fixed and cleared.

causes2.name: ABS actuator or VDC control unit fault
causes2.tell: The lights never clear, the codes point inside the unit itself, and the brake pedal may pulse oddly at low speed.
causes2.fix: The ABS and VDC actuator or control unit is replaced and then set up for your car with a scan tool.

slip-indicator-light.shop: A shop starts with a scan tool that can read the ABS and VDC modules, not just engine codes, and pulls the stored faults. They check battery voltage, read the engine codes too, since an engine fault alone will shut VDC off, then watch all four wheel speed signals in live data on a short test drive to see which one drops out. Diagnosis normally runs half an hour to an hour, longer when the fault only shows up now and then.

reset.how: These are fault indicators, not a service reminder, so there is nothing you are meant to reset after a job. Clearing the codes turns the lights off briefly, but the system switches them straight back on when it sees the same problem. The one genuine procedure is the relearn after the battery has been disconnected or has gone flat: drive straight above about 10 mph for at least ten minutes and the lights should go out on their own. If they are still lit after that, the system has found a real fault that needs repairing.
reset.note: Pressing the VDC OFF button only switches the system off and on, it does not clear a stored fault.

faqs.q: Is it safe to drive with the SLIP and VDC OFF lights on?
faqs.a: Your brakes, steering and engine still work, but the electronic help that catches a slide is missing. Take it gently, especially in rain, snow or on gravel, where the car is noticeably less forgiving. Leave more room and get the fault read. If the ABS or red brake light is on too, get it checked before driving further.

faqs.q: Why did the SLIP and VDC OFF lights come on after I changed my battery?
faqs.a: The system lost its memory of where straight ahead is. Nissan's fix is to drive straight on a level road at more than about 10 mph for at least ten minutes, which lets it relearn. If the lights are still on after that drive, something else is wrong and the codes need reading.

faqs.q: My SLIP light only blinks in the rain, is that a problem?
faqs.a: No, that is the system doing its job. A blinking SLIP light means a wheel started to spin and the car stepped in. Treat it as a warning that the road is slicker than it looks: ease off the accelerator and keep your steering smooth.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the SLIP or VDC OFF light on?
faqs.a: The SLIP and VDC OFF lights are not emissions lights, so they do not usually fail the computer part of an emissions test on their own. A state safety inspection can fail a car with the ABS light on alongside them. Rules vary by state, so check what yours tests.

faqs.q: Can a bad wheel bearing or one odd tire set these lights off?
faqs.a: Yes to both. The wheel speed sensor often lives in the wheel bearing on these cars, so a worn bearing can take the signal with it. A spare or mismatched tire makes one wheel turn at a different speed, and the computer reads that as something wrong.

tire-pressure-light.look: An amber light low in the instrument cluster shaped like a cross section of a tire, a flat bottomed horseshoe with an exclamation mark inside it. People often mistake it for a jar, a horseshoe or a cup. Some makes add the letters TPMS, or show a message such as CHECK TIRE PRESSURE or LOW TIRE PRESSURE, and many newer cars will also show the pressure at each wheel on a screen in the cluster or the center display.
tire-pressure-light.flash: A flashing light means something different from a steady one. If it blinks for about a minute every time you start the car and then stays on solid, the system itself is at fault, usually a dead sensor in a wheel or sensors that were never matched to the car. Your tires may be perfectly fine, but the car can no longer warn you if one goes low, so you have to check them by hand.

diy.t: Check all four tires with a gauge when they are cold
diy.how: Do this before you drive, or after the car has sat at least three hours, because rolling heats the air and hides a low tire. Unscrew the cap on the valve stem, push the gauge straight on until the hissing stops, and read the number. Compare it with the figure on the sticker in the driver's door opening, not the much higher number moulded into the tire sidewall. Add air a little at a time and recheck.

diy.t: Find a slow leak with soapy water
diy.how: Mix a squirt of dish soap into a cup of water and brush or pour it over the tread, around the wheel rim and over the valve stem of the tire that keeps going down. Watch for a patch of small bubbles that keeps growing, which marks the hole. Mark the spot with chalk or tape so the tire shop can find it straight away. A nail head often looks like a harmless dark speck until you get close.

diy.t: Don't forget the spare
diy.how: On many trucks, SUVs and vans the full size spare has its own sensor, so a soft spare can light the dash while all four tires on the ground are fine. Check your owner's manual to see whether yours is monitored, then check its pressure the same way. A spare that has sat for years is almost always low, and that is also worth knowing before you need it.

diy.t: Clear the light once the pressures are right
diy.how: On many cars the light goes out by itself after some driving once every tire is at the door-sticker pressure. Others need a reset from a button, a menu or a shop scan tool, and the steps and timing differ by make, model and year, so follow your owner's manual or the make-specific steps on this page. If the light blinks for a minute at every start instead, no amount of driving will clear it.

dont: Don't inflate to the big number on the tire sidewall, that is the maximum the tire can hold, not what your car wants.
Don't keep driving on a tire that looks flat or squashed at the bottom, even for a mile, as the sidewall breaks up from the inside.
Don't just reset the light and carry on without putting a gauge on all four tires.
Don't ignore a light that keeps coming back every few weeks, that is a slow leak and slow leaks turn into blowouts.

causes2.name: Simply low on air, often from cold weather
causes2.tell: All four tires read a few pounds low, and the light appeared on the first cold morning of the season or after a long spell of not driving. Tires lose a little air through the rubber every month on their own, and pressure falls by roughly one pound for every ten degrees the temperature drops. Nothing else is wrong.
causes2.fix: Add air to the pressure on the driver's door sticker and the light goes out on its own after a short drive.

causes2.name: Nail, screw or other puncture
causes2.tell: One tire only, and it keeps going down over days or hours while the other three hold steady. Soapy water bubbles at one spot in the tread. Very common after driving past building work or a parking lot being resurfaced.
causes2.fix: A tire shop takes the tire off the wheel and fits a patch plug from the inside, which is a permanent repair in the middle of the tread. Damage in the sidewall or shoulder cannot be repaired safely and needs a new tire.

causes2.name: Leaking or corroded valve stem
causes2.tell: One tire goes soft with no nail anywhere in the tread, and the bubbles form right at the metal or rubber stem you put air into. Rubber stems go hard and crack with age, and the metal ones used with sensors corrode where road salt sits. Often shows up on cars around seven years old.
causes2.fix: The tire is taken off the wheel and a new stem or sensor service kit is fitted, which is usually done at the same time as a rotation.

causes2.name: Sensor with a dead battery
causes2.tell: This is the flashing then solid light. The sensors are sealed units with a battery inside that lasts around seven to ten years, so they start dying one after another on an older car, often within a year of each other. The pressures are correct when you check them by hand.
causes2.fix: A tire shop breaks the tire bead, swaps in a new sensor and matches it to the car.

causes2.name: Sensors never matched to the car
causes2.tell: The light came on straight after new tires, a rotation, a seasonal wheel swap or a repair, and the pressures are all fine. Some cars learn the new positions by themselves after a few miles, others need a tool, and winter wheel sets with their own sensors need the swap registered each time.
causes2.fix: The shop runs a relearn with a scan tool so the car knows which sensor is at which corner. If the tires were just fitted somewhere, go back there first and ask them to do it.

causes2.name: Fault in the receiver or module
causes2.tell: The least common cause by a long way. New sensors were fitted and the light still blinks, or the car reads no signal at all from any wheel. Can follow water getting into a control unit or a damaged antenna wire.
causes2.fix: The receiver or module is tested, then replaced and programmed to the car.

tire-pressure-light.shop: At a tire shop the first move is a gauge on all four tires and the spare, then a look for a nail and a water tank dunk to find a leak you cannot see. That part is often quick. If the light blinks before it goes solid, they use a TPMS tool instead, which wakes each sensor in turn and shows its pressure, temperature and battery state, so a dead sensor and an unregistered one are told apart in a few minutes.

reset.how: Fix the pressure first, then reset only if your car needs it. Set every tire, and the spare if yours is monitored, to the cold pressure on the driver's door sticker. On many cars the light then goes out by itself after some driving; others need a reset from a button, a menu or a shop scan tool. The exact steps and timing differ by make, model, year and equipment, so follow your owner's manual or the make-specific steps below. If a tire is damaged or keeps losing air, fix the tire first. If the light flashes for about a minute (60–90 seconds) at startup and then stays on, the monitoring system has a fault: a reset won't fix it.
reset.note: The procedure varies a lot by make, model and year, and some vehicles will only relearn with a shop scan tool. Your owner's manual has the one for your car.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the tire pressure light on?
faqs.a: If a tire looks low, bulges at the bottom, or the car pulls or feels vague in corners, stop and put the spare on or call for a tow. A tire run badly low gets hot and can come apart at speed. If the tires only feel a little soft and look normal, drive slowly to the nearest air pump and set them to the pressure on the driver's door sticker.

faqs.q: Does the tire pressure light reset itself?
faqs.a: Yes, in most cases. Once the pressures are correct the car sees the good readings and turns the light off after a short drive, usually within twenty minutes. If it does not clear after that, either a tire is still low or a sensor is at fault.

faqs.q: Why did it come on when it got cold?
faqs.a: Air shrinks as it cools, so pressure drops by about one pound for every ten degree fall in temperature. A tire that was fine in the fall can trip the warning on the first freezing morning. Top them up to the door sticker figure and they will be slightly high on a hot day, which is normal and expected.

faqs.q: Will it pass inspection?
faqs.a: In most states a tire pressure light on its own does not fail an inspection, though inspectors will almost always measure your tread depth and check the tires anyway. A few states that run a full safety check will note it. Worn out or damaged tires are a far more common reason to fail than the light itself.

faqs.q: Can I just have the sensors turned off?
faqs.a: Some scan tools can switch the system off on some vehicles, but it is a bad trade. You lose your only early warning of a slow leak, which matters most on a car with no spare.

transmission-warning-light.look: Usually in the middle of the instrument cluster: a cog or gear outline with an exclamation mark inside it, or the same gear with a small thermometer through it. Many makes show no symbol at all and print a message instead, such as 'Transmission hot', 'AT oil temp' or 'Service transmission'. Hondas and Acuras often flash the D or D4 gear letter on the gauge rather than lighting a separate light.
transmission-warning-light.flash: A flashing gear symbol, or a flashing D, D4 or O/D OFF indicator, nearly always means the transmission computer has stored a fault and has put the car into a protected mode. Treat a flashing light as more urgent than a steady one, keep your speed down and stay off the accelerator.

diy.t: Read the exact wording in the driver display
diy.how: Scroll through the message on the dash or the small screen between the gauges. 'Transmission hot' or 'AT oil temp' is a heat warning and means stop and let it cool. 'Service transmission', or a plain gear symbol with no message, is a stored fault and means drive gently to a shop. Those two need completely different responses, so the thirty seconds it takes to read the screen is worth it.

diy.t: Let it cool if the warning mentions heat
diy.how: Pull into a safe spot off the road and do what the message or your owner's manual says. Many cars want you to idle in Park with the air conditioning off for fifteen to twenty minutes; some, including several Ford models, tell you to turn the engine off instead. If the warning clears, drive gently and stay off long climbs and heavy loads until it has been checked.

diy.t: Check the transmission fluid if there is a dipstick
diy.how: Many cars built in the last fifteen years have no transmission dipstick, and checking those is a shop job. If yours has one it is usually a ring-pull handle toward the back of the engine bay, marked for transmission fluid. Park on level ground with the parking brake set and follow the exact steps in your owner's manual, because some makes read it cold and some read it warm. Healthy fluid is pink or red and barely smells; dark brown fluid that smells burnt is a real finding.

diy.t: Look for red fluid spots where you park
diy.how: Transmission fluid is dyed red or pink, while engine oil is brown or black, so a red patch on the driveway points straight at the transmission or one of its cooler lines. Check the spot where the car normally sits overnight rather than crawling anywhere. Take a photo of it, because the size and color tell a shop a lot before they even open the hood.

dont: Don't keep towing or climbing hills with a transmission heat warning showing. Heat is what destroys a transmission.
Don't hold the accelerator down trying to force the car out of limp mode. It is protecting itself, and you are adding heat.
Don't just clear the code and carry on. The fault is still there and the light will come back.
Don't let a shop sell you a fluid flush as a first guess before anyone has read the transmission's own codes.

causes2.name: Low, old or burnt transmission fluid
causes2.tell: Shifts feel late, harsh or slip under load, and the warning often shows up first on a hot day or after towing. Fluid on the dipstick is dark brown instead of red and smells burnt. The car may have no record of a fluid service, or there may be red drips where it parks.
causes2.fix: Drain and refill with the exact fluid the maker specifies, and replace the filter and pan gasket on transmissions that have a serviceable one. Any leak has to be found and sealed first, or the level just drops again.

causes2.name: Failed shift solenoid or solenoid pack
causes2.tell: The car gets stuck in one gear, skips a gear, or shifts at the wrong engine speed, and it usually stores a code in the P0750 to P0770 group along with a general P0700. Often comes and goes when cold and becomes constant as it warms up.
causes2.fix: Replace the faulty solenoid, or the whole solenoid pack where they are sold as one unit. Most sit behind the transmission pan or the side cover, so the job includes fresh fluid and a gasket.

causes2.name: Bad input or output speed sensor
causes2.tell: The speedometer may flicker or drop to zero, cruise control stops working, and shifts turn hard because the computer has lost track of how fast the shafts are turning. Codes usually point at a specific sensor circuit rather than the whole transmission.
causes2.fix: Replace the sensor, which normally bolts into the outside of the transmission case, and clear the codes.

causes2.name: Valve body or pressure control fault
causes2.tell: Harsh bangs between gears, a long delay before the car moves after you select Drive, or flaring where the engine revs between shifts. Codes often mention pressure control or a specific gear ratio being wrong.
causes2.fix: The valve body is the hydraulic control block inside the transmission. Shops either rebuild it or fit a replacement unit, then refill the transmission and relearn the shift settings.

causes2.name: Wiring, connector or control module fault
causes2.tell: The warning appears and disappears for no obvious reason, sometimes with several unrelated codes at once, and often after work was done nearby or after the car sat wet. Shaking the harness or driving over bumps can bring it on.
causes2.fix: The shop traces the circuit, repairs the chafed wire, corroded pin or water-filled connector, and only replaces the transmission control module if the wiring is proved good.

causes2.name: Internal wear or damage
causes2.tell: The worst case, and usually the one with the longest history: slipping that has been getting worse for months, a whine or growl that changes with road speed, metal glitter in the fluid, or the car refusing to move in one direction. Codes about wrong gear ratios keep returning after repairs.
causes2.fix: A rebuild or a replacement transmission, remanufactured or used.

transmission-warning-light.shop: A shop starts with a scan tool, reading the transmission computer's own codes rather than just the generic engine ones, because a general transmission code only says 'look in here for the real code'. Then they watch live data while the car drives: fluid temperature, which gear the computer asked for, which gear it actually got, and the shaft speed readings. They check the fluid level and condition, look for leaks and inspect the wiring at the transmission. On a car that still drives normally, expect about an hour. A fault that only appears once everything is hot can take two hours or more.

reset.how: This is a fault light, not a service reminder, so there is nothing you are meant to reset. A scan tool will switch it off, but that repairs nothing: the transmission computer sets it again as soon as it sees the same problem, often within a few miles. Disconnecting the battery can also wipe the transmission's learned shift settings, which makes the car feel different for a day or two and fools people into thinking it is fixed. Repair the cause and the light goes out by itself.
reset.note: What this light covers and how it behaves differ a lot between makes, so check your owner's manual for the wording your car uses.

faqs.q: How long can I drive with the transmission warning light on?
faqs.a: If it is a heat warning, stop now and let it cool, because heat is what ruins a transmission. If it is a fault warning and the car still drives, you can usually get it home or to a shop driving gently, but do not keep using it for weeks. Faults that start small, like low fluid or one bad solenoid, turn into rebuilds when they are ignored.

faqs.q: What is limp mode?
faqs.a: Limp mode is the car protecting itself. The computer locks the transmission into one gear, usually second or third, and caps how fast the engine will rev, so the car feels gutless and will not go much above highway merging speed. It is deliberate, not extra damage, and it is telling you to drive straight to a shop.

faqs.q: Will my car pass inspection with the transmission light on?
faqs.a: It depends where you live. The transmission light itself is not usually on the inspection list, but a stored transmission fault normally turns the check engine light on as well, and in states with an emissions check an illuminated check engine light is an automatic fail. Get it read before you book the test.

faqs.q: Does the transmission light reset itself?
faqs.a: A heat warning goes out on its own once the fluid cools down. A stored fault will not: it stays on, or flickers on and off as the problem comes and goes, until the cause is repaired. If it clears by itself and then returns, write down when it happens, because that pattern helps a shop find it.

faqs.q: Could it just be low transmission fluid?
faqs.a: But transmissions do not burn fluid the way engines burn oil, so if the level is low it has leaked out somewhere. Topping it up without finding the leak just buys you a few months.

water-in-fuel-light.look: It sits in the main instrument cluster, is always amber, and only appears on diesels. Most makes draw a fuel filter canister with a drain tap at the bottom and water droplets in it. Many American diesel trucks skip the picture and simply spell out WATER IN FUEL or DRAIN FUEL FILTER in the message screen between the gauges.

diy.t: Drain the water separator
diy.how: Check the owner's manual first: it shows where the drain is, and some trucks say not to restart until the water is drained. With the engine off and cold, find the fuel filter canister; most diesel pickups have a drain valve on the bottom.
